name: Red 40
scoreRationale: Legal and within ADI for most people, but linked to hyperactivity in some children, carries an EU warning label, and is being phased out of U.S. school foods.
summary: Red 40 is the most-used synthetic food dye in the U.S. It's purely cosmetic, and evidence that it affects some children's behavior is driving new restrictions.

physical.phStability: Stable across food pH; resists light and heat

overview: Allura Red AC (Red 40) is an azo dye: two aromatic ring systems connected by an azo bridge (–N=N–). The azo group links the rings into one long conjugated system of alternating double bonds, which absorbs blue-green light (around 504 nm) so we see red.

Two sulfonate groups (–SO₃⁻ Na⁺) make the dye very water-soluble and keep it from being absorbed well in the gut. Food makers favor it because it is cheap, bright and stable to heat, light and acid, unlike many natural red pigments.
profile.function: Colors candy, drinks, cereals, snacks and cosmetics a bright, consistent red with no flavor or nutritional role.

mechanisms.title: Why it looks red
mechanisms.chemical: Electrons in the conjugated π system absorb light of about 504 nm (blue-green) and jump to a higher energy level.
mechanisms.biological: Our eyes see the complementary, unabsorbed wavelengths, which appear red.

mechanisms.title: Breakdown by gut bacteria
mechanisms.chemical: Azoreductase enzymes made by colon bacteria cleave the –N=N– bond, producing two sulfonated aromatic amines.
mechanisms.biological: These products are poorly absorbed and mostly excreted. The sulfonate groups make them far less toxic than unsulfonated aromatic amines.

mechanisms.title: Behavior in sensitive children
mechanisms.chemical: No single mechanism is established; hypotheses include effects on neurotransmitters and histamine release.
mechanisms.biological: Randomized trials, notably the 2007 Southampton study, found that dye mixtures containing Red 40 increased hyperactive behavior in some children. California's 2021 review concluded synthetic dyes can affect behavior in some children.

mechanisms.title: Gut inflammation in mice
mechanisms.chemical: In a 2022 mouse study, long-term Red 40 exposure increased serotonin production by cells lining the gut.
mechanisms.biological: The mice developed more severe experimental colitis. Whether this happens in people is unknown.

reactions.title: Diazotization and azo coupling (how it's made)
reactions.summary: Two classic reactions stitch the dye together.

steps.name: Diazotization
steps.text: An aromatic amine (cresidine-4-sulfonic acid) reacts with nitrous acid near 0 °C, forming a reactive diazonium ion (Ar–N₂⁺).

steps.name: Azo coupling
steps.text: The diazonium ion attacks the electron-rich ring of a naphthol (Schaeffer's salt) in an electrophilic aromatic substitution.

steps.name: Isolation
steps.text: The dye is salted out, purified and dried.

reactions.result: The new –N=N– bridge joins the two rings into one conjugated system, which is what creates the color.

reactions.title: Azo reduction
reactions.summary: Breaking the azo bridge destroys the color.

steps.name: Electron transfer
steps.text: Bacterial azoreductase passes electrons from NADH to the azo group.

steps.name: Intermediate
steps.text: The –N=N– bond becomes a single-bonded hydrazo group (–NH–NH–).

steps.name: Cleavage
steps.text: Further reduction splits it into two separate amines.

reactions.result: The same reaction lets bacteria in wastewater treatment decolorize azo dyes.

regulatory.status: Certified color additive; FDA announced in 2025 a plan to phase out petroleum-based dyes, relying largely on industry commitments.
Authorized as E129 but foods must carry the warning "may have an adverse effect on activity and attention in children".
The School Food Safety Act (2024) bans Red 40 in public-school foods from the end of 2027.
ADI 0–7 mg/kg body weight.

hazards.title: Hyperactivity in sensitive children
hazards.summary: Not a cause of ADHD, but a measurable effect in some children.
hazards.chemical: The underlying mechanism remains unclear.
hazards.biological: Effects in trials were small on average but larger in some individuals, which led the EU to require warning labels and California to remove dyes from school food.

hazards.title: Manufacturing impurities
hazards.summary: Controlled by batch testing.
hazards.chemical: Synthesis can leave trace aromatic amines such as benzidine, a known carcinogen.
hazards.biological: FDA certifies every batch sold in the U.S. and limits these impurities to parts per billion.

profile.dosage: U.S. children's intakes can approach several mg/kg on high-candy days; average intakes are below the ADI.

myths.claim: Red 40 is made from bugs.
myths.consensus: That's carmine (cochineal). Red 40 is synthesized from petroleum-derived chemicals.

myths.claim: Red 40 causes ADHD.
myths.consensus: It doesn't cause ADHD, but evidence suggests it can worsen hyperactive behavior in some sensitive children.

environment.persistence: Moderately persistent; azo dyes resist aerobic breakdown.

synthesis.title: Petrochemical synthesis
synthesis.summary: Made from aromatic chemicals derived from petroleum.
synthesis.mechanism: Cresidine-4-sulfonic acid is diazotized with sodium nitrite and acid, then coupled with 6-hydroxy-2-naphthalenesulfonic acid. The disodium salt is precipitated, washed and dried.
synthesis.significance: Every batch sold in the U.S. is chemically tested and certified by FDA before use.

citations.title: Squid pen chitin chitooligomers as food colorants absorbers.
citations.abstract: One of the most promising applications of chitosanase is the conversion of chitinous biowaste into bioactive chitooligomers (COS). TKU033 chitosanase was induced from squid pen powder (SPP)-containing Bacillus cereus TKU033 medium and purified by ammonium sulfate precipitation and column chromatography. The enzyme was relatively more thermostable in the presence of the substrate and had an activity of 93% at 50 °C in a pH 5 buffer solution for 60 min. Furthermore, the enzyme used for the COS preparation was also studied. The enzyme products revealed various mixtures of COS that with different degrees of polymerization (DP), ranging from three to nine. In the culture medium, the fermented SPP was recovered, and it displayed a better adsorption rate (up to 96%) for the disperse dyes than the water-soluble food colorants, Allura Red AC (R40) and Tartrazne (Y4). Fourier transform-infrared spectroscopic (FT-IR) analysis proved that the adsorption of the dyes onto fermented SPP was a physical adsorption. Results also showed that fermented SPP was a favorable adsorber and could be employed as low-cost alternative for dye removal in wastewater treatment.

citations.title: Food dyes as P-glycoprotein modulators.
citations.abstract: The drug transporter P-glycoprotein (P-gp) is often investigated in drug-interaction studies because the activity is modulated by a wide variety of xenobiotics including drugs, herbal products, and food components. In this study, we tested six common arylsulfonate food dyes-allura red, carmoisine, ponceau 4R, quinolone yellow, sunset yellow, and tartrazine-as activators and inhibitors of P-gp activity in vitro. The dyes were studied as P-gp activators by measuring ATPase activity in P-gp-expressing membranes. Compared to verapamil, a known activator of P-gp, the six food dyes showed no stimulatory activity. The potential for these six food dyes to act as P-gp inhibitors was tested in an intracellular efflux assay with P-gp-expressing cells. Compared to GF120918, a known P-gp inhibitor, there was no inhibitory activity for these six food dyes. The six food dyes tested do not interact with P-gp in vitro and, therefore, are unlikely cause clinical drug-food dye interactions. Further investigation is necessary to determine whether these food dyes could interact with other drug transporters.

citations.title: Food Safety and Health Concerns of Synthetic Food Colors: An Update.
citations.abstract: The toxicity of food additives is widely studied and concerns many consumers worldwide. Synthetic food colors are often considered an unnecessary risk to consumer health. Since the European Food Safety Authority's (EFSA) re-evaluation between 2009 and 2014, the body of scientific literature on food colors has grown, and new evaluations are being published by the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (JECFA). Therefore, this narrative review aims to review the toxicological data that have become available since 2014. The reviewed colors are Quinoline Yellow, Sunset Yellow, Azorubine, Amaranth, Ponceau 4R, Erythrosine, Allura Red, Patent Blue, Indigo Carmine, Brilliant Blue FCF, Green S, Brilliant Black, Brown HT, and Lithol Rubine BK. Tartrazine was not included in this paper; the overwhelming amount of recent data on Tartrazine toxicity requires more space than this review can provide. The issues regarding the toxicity of synthetic food colors and real population exposures are being regularly examined and reviewed by relevant authorities, such as the EFSA and JECFA. The current ADI limits set by the authorities are mostly in agreement, and they seem safe. However, the EFSA and JECFA assessments of some of the colors are more than a decade old, and new evidence will soon be required.

citations.title: Health safety issues of synthetic food colorants.
citations.abstract: Increasing attention has been recently paid to the toxicity of additives used in food. The European Parliament and the Council published the REGULATION (EC) No. 1333/2008 on food additives establishing that the toxicity of food additives evaluated before 20th January 2009 must be re-evaluated by European Food Safety Authority (EFSA). The aim of this review is to survey current knowledge specifically on the toxicity issues of synthetic food colorants using official reports published by the EFSA and other available studies published since the respective report. Synthetic colorants described are Tartrazine, Quinoline Yellow, Sunset Yellow, Azorubine, Ponceau 4R, Erythrosine, Allura Red, Patent Blue, Indigo Carmine, Brilliant Blue FCF, Green S, Brilliant Black and Brown HT. Moreover, a summary of evidence on possible detrimental effects of colorant mixes on children's behaviour is provided and future research directions are outlined.

name: Yellow 5
scoreRationale: Must be named on U.S. labels due to intolerance reactions, carries the EU hyperactivity warning, and is included in new school-food bans.
summary: Yellow 5 is a synthetic lemon-yellow dye. A small number of people react to it, and it's part of the dye group linked to hyperactivity in some children.

physical.phStability: Stable in acidic foods; good light fastness

overview: Tartrazine (Yellow 5) is a lemon-yellow azo dye built from a pyrazolone ring and two sulfonated benzene rings, linked by an azo group (–N=N–). Its conjugated system absorbs violet-blue light (about 427 nm), so we see yellow.
Its sulfonate groups make it water-soluble and poorly absorbed. Mixed with a blue dye such as Brilliant Blue, it makes the bright greens of candies and sports drinks.
profile.function: Colors soft drinks, candies, chips, pickles, soaps and cosmetics yellow or, mixed with blue, green.

mechanisms.title: Why it looks yellow
mechanisms.chemical: The dye's conjugated electrons absorb light around 427 nm, in the violet-blue part of the spectrum.
mechanisms.biological: The light that remains, which our eyes see, appears bright yellow.

mechanisms.title: Intolerance reactions
mechanisms.chemical: In a small group of people, tartrazine appears to activate mast cells and inflammatory pathways without IgE antibodies (a pseudo-allergic reaction).
mechanisms.biological: Hives, itching or asthma symptoms can result; many affected people are also sensitive to aspirin.

mechanisms.title: Gut bacterial breakdown
mechanisms.chemical: Colon bacteria cleave the azo bond, producing sulfanilic acid and an aminopyrazolone.
mechanisms.biological: Both products are largely excreted without accumulating.

reactions.title: Azo coupling (how it's made)
reactions.summary: The dye is assembled from two pieces.

steps.name: Diazotization
steps.text: Sulfanilic acid reacts with nitrous acid to form a diazonium ion.

steps.name: Coupling
steps.text: The diazonium ion attacks a sulfophenyl pyrazolone carboxylic acid.

steps.name: Salt formation
steps.text: The product is isolated as its trisodium salt.

reactions.result: The pyrazolone ring shifts the absorption toward shorter wavelengths, giving yellow instead of red.

regulatory.status: Certified color; must be declared by name on labels because of intolerance reports.
Authorized as E102 with the mandatory hyperactivity warning label.
Banned in public-school foods from the end of 2027 (AB 2316).

hazards.title: Intolerance in a small minority
hazards.summary: Why U.S. labels must name Yellow 5 specifically.
hazards.chemical: Pseudo-allergic activation of mast cells releases histamine and other mediators.
hazards.biological: Reactions include hives and, rarely, asthma attacks; estimates suggest well under 1 in 1,000 people are affected.

hazards.title: Hyperactivity in sensitive children
hazards.summary: Included in the dye mixtures tested in the Southampton trial.
hazards.chemical: The mechanism is not established.
hazards.biological: The EU requires a warning about effects on children's activity and attention on foods containing it.

profile.dosage: JECFA ADI is 0–10 mg/kg body weight; typical exposure is lower.

myths.claim: Yellow 5 lowers sperm count.
myths.consensus: This long-running rumor about neon sodas has no supporting human evidence.

myths.claim: Yellow 5 is banned in Europe.
myths.consensus: It is permitted in the EU, but products must carry a warning about children's activity and attention.

synthesis.title: Industrial synthesis
synthesis.summary: A classic azo coupling.
synthesis.mechanism: Sulfanilic acid is diazotized and coupled with 1-(4-sulfophenyl)-3-carboxy-5-pyrazolone, then the dye is isolated as the trisodium salt and purified.
synthesis.significance: Johann Heinrich Ziegler first made tartrazine in 1884 during the boom in synthetic dyes.

citations.title: Experimental and theoretical study of dyes adsorption process on chitosan-based cryogel.
citations.abstract: In this research, the adsorption of three synthetic dyes dissolved in an aqueous solution on chitosan cryogel beads (Q-C-EGDE) was compared. The effect of the pH of the solution on the adsorption capacity of each dyes was analyzed. Furthermore, the kinetics and adsorption isotherms were compared, at temperatures of 283.15 K, 303.15 K and 323.15 K, and the kinetic and adsorption equilibrium data were fitted to three mathematical models, respectively. The biosorbent was characterized by scanning electron microscopy (SEM), the nitrogen physisorption BET method and Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR). The characterization results show that the cryogel is composed of low-surface, macroporous, porous grooved walls. The functional groups that took part in the adsorption were mainly amino groups (NH3+). When comparing the adsorption capacities, it was found that the dyes adsorb in the following order Blue 1 > Red 2 > Yellow 5 reaching capacities from 1600 mg/L to 850 mg/L. The results of the adsorption and mathematical modelling suggest that the process is regulated mainly by physisorption and is largely limited by mass transfer mechanisms within the cryogel, where the electrostatic charges present affect adsorption. The latter was corroborated by the Monte Carlo simulation.

citations.title: Enhanced decolorization of dyes by an iron modified clay and thermodynamic parameters.
citations.abstract: The sorption processes of red 5 (R5) and yellow 5 (Y5) dyes by iron modified and sodium bentonite in aqueous solutions was evaluated. The modified clay was prepared, conditioned and characterized. The sodium clay did not remove any of either dye. The sorption kinetics and isotherms of R5 and Y5 dyes by iron modified clay were determined. The maximum removal percentages achieved were 97% and 98% for R5 and Y5, respectively, and a contact time of 72 h; the experimental data were best adjusted to Ho model. The isotherms of both dyes were best adjusted to the Langmuir model and the maximum adsorption capacities of the modified clay were 11.26 mg/g and 5.28 mg/g for R5 and Y5, respectively. These results indicate that adsorption processes have a high probability to be described as chemisorption on a homogeneous material. Temperature range between 283 and 213 K does not affect the adsorption of Y5 by the iron modified clay, but the adsorption process of R5 was affected, and the thermodynamic parameters could be calculated, which indicate a chemisorption mechanism.

citations.title: Toxicology of food dyes.
citations.abstract: Background: Food dyes, synthesized originally from coal tar and now petroleum, have long been controversial because of safety concerns. Many dyes have been banned because of their adverse effects on laboratory animals or inadequate testing. Conclusions: This review finds that all of the nine currently US-approved dyes raise health concerns of varying degrees. Red 3 causes cancer in animals, and there is evidence that several other dyes also are carcinogenic. Three dyes (Red 40, Yellow 5, and Yellow 6) have been found to be contaminated with benzidine or other carcinogens. At least four dyes (Blue 1, Red 40, Yellow 5, and Yellow 6) cause hypersensitivity reactions. Numerous microbiological and rodent studies of Yellow 5 were positive for genotoxicity. Toxicity tests on two dyes (Citrus Red 2 and Orange B) also suggest safety concerns, but Citrus Red 2 is used at low levels and only on some Florida oranges and Orange B has not been used for several years. The inadequacy of much of the testing and the evidence for carcinogenicity, genotoxicity, and hypersensitivity, coupled with the fact that dyes do not improve the safety or nutritional quality of foods, indicates that all of the currently used dyes should be removed from the food supply and replaced, if at all, by safer colorings. It is recommended that regulatory authorities require better and independent toxicity testing, exercise greater caution regarding continued approval of these dyes, and in the future approve only well-tested, safe dyes.

citations.title: HC Yellow 5.
citations.abstract: The Expert Panel for Cosmetic Ingredient Safety reviewed updated information that has become available since their original assessment from 2007, along with updated information regarding product types, and frequency and concentrations of use, and reaffirmed their original conclusion that HC Yellow 5 is safe as a hair dye ingredient in the practices of use and concentration as described in this report.

citations.title: Application of the IOC Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) Clinical Assessment Tool version 2 (CAT2) across 200+ elite athletes.
citations.abstract: Objective: This cross-sectional retrospective and prospective study implemented the 2023 International Olympic Committee Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs) Clinical Assessment Tool version 2 (CAT2) to determine the current severity of REDs (primary outcome) and future risk of bone stress injuries (BSI, exploratory outcome) in elite athletes. Methods: Female (n=143; 23.3±4.3 years) and male (n=70; 23.1±3.7 years) athletes (performance tier 3 (52%), tier 4 (36%), tier 5 (12%)) participated in a baseline CAT2 (with minor modifications) assessment, including a self-report questionnaire (menstrual function (females), BSI, Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q)), bone mineral density (BMD via DXA) and fasted blood analysis (triiodothyronine (T3), testosterone, cholesterol). Athletes were assigned a green, yellow, orange or red light via CAT2. The prospective risk of new self-report of physician-diagnosed BSI was assessed over a subsequent 6-24 months. Results: REDs prevalence was 55% green, 36% yellow, 5% orange and 4% red light. The CAT2 identified a greater prevalence of amenorrhoea and BSI and lower T3, testosterone and BMD (p<0.01) in red, orange and yellow (those with REDs) versus green light. ORs for a prospective self-reported BSI (majority physician diagnosed) were greater in orange vs green (OR 7.71, 95% CI (1.26 to 39.83)), in females with severe amenorrhoea (OR 4.6 (95% CI 0.98 to 17.85)), in males with low sex drive (OR 16.0 (95% CI 4.79 to 1038.87)), and athletes with elevated EDE-Q global scores (OR 1.45 (95% CI 0.97 to 1.97)). Conclusion: The CAT2 has high validity in demonstrating current severity of REDs, with increased future risk of self-reported BSI in athletes with a more severe REDs traffic light category.

name: Caramel Color
scoreRationale: Plain caramel (class I) is benign, but ammonia-process caramels (classes III/IV, used in colas) contain 4-MEI, a possible carcinogen now kept low under California rules.
summary: Caramel color gives colas, sauces and gravies their brown hue. Most types are harmless; the ammonia-made kinds contain a by-product regulators limit.

identity.composition: Complex mixture of polymers from heated carbohydrates. Class I (plain), II (caustic sulfite), III (ammonia) and IV (sulfite-ammonia).

physical.phStability: Classes are matched to product pH (class IV for acidic colas)

overview: Caramel color is a complex mixture of brown polymers made by heating sugars under controlled conditions. Unlike a single dye molecule, it contains thousands of different molecules, from small flavor compounds to large colored polymers called melanoidins.

Manufacturers sort it into four classes by what is added during heating: plain (I), caustic sulfite (II), ammonia (III) and sulfite-ammonia (IV). The additives control the particles' electric charge, which matters: a cola needs a negatively charged caramel (class IV) that won't clump in its acidic environment.
profile.function: Provides consistent brown color in colas, soy sauce, beer, gravy, baked goods and some hair and skin products.

mechanisms.title: Why it's brown
mechanisms.chemical: Dehydrated sugar fragments link into large conjugated polymers that absorb light across the visible spectrum, more strongly at blue wavelengths.
mechanisms.biological: We see the mixture as brown; manufacturers measure its strength as “tinctorial power”.

mechanisms.title: Matching the charge
mechanisms.chemical: Ammonium and sulfite reactants give caramel particles a positive or negative surface charge.
mechanisms.biological: Matching the charge to the drink or sauce keeps the color evenly dispersed; a mismatch causes haze or sediment.

mechanisms.title: 4-MEI in animal studies
mechanisms.chemical: In class III and IV caramels, ammonia reacts with sugar fragments such as methylglyoxal to form 4-methylimidazole (4-MEI).
mechanisms.biological: In a U.S. National Toxicology Program study, high doses of 4-MEI caused lung tumors in mice but not rats; IARC classifies it as possibly carcinogenic.

reactions.title: Ammonia caramel chemistry
reactions.summary: A Maillard-type reaction between sugar fragments and ammonia.

steps.name: Fragmentation
steps.text: Heated sugars dehydrate and split into small reactive dicarbonyls such as methylglyoxal.

steps.name: Ring formation
steps.text: Ammonia reacts with these dicarbonyls to form imidazoles, including 4-MEI.

steps.name: Polymerization
steps.text: Fragments link into large brown melanoidins that carry the color.

reactions.result: Controlling time, temperature and reactants lets manufacturers minimize 4-MEI while hitting a target color.

regulatory.status: Color additive exempt from certification.
4-MEI is listed; beverages over 29 µg/day exposure need a warning, which led major colas to reduce 4-MEI levels in 2012.
Set ADIs of 100–300 mg/kg body weight depending on class.

hazards.title: 4-MEI byproduct
hazards.summary: Applies to ammonia-process caramels (classes III and IV), used in colas.
hazards.chemical: 4-MEI forms when ammonia reacts with sugar fragments during heating.
hazards.biological: California's Prop 65 listing led major cola makers to cut 4-MEI levels in 2012; exposure today is far below levels that caused effects in mice.

profile.dosage: Exposure depends heavily on cola consumption; reformulated U.S. colas contain much lower 4-MEI than before 2012.

myths.claim: Caramel color is just burnt sugar.
myths.consensus: Class I is, but classes III and IV are made with ammonia compounds that create by-products like 4-MEI.

synthesis.title: Industrial cooking
synthesis.summary: Controlled caramelization at scale.
synthesis.mechanism: Food-grade glucose or sucrose syrup is heated, often under pressure, with food-grade acids, alkalis, ammonium compounds or sulfites. When the target color intensity is reached, the batch is cooled and filtered.
synthesis.significance: Plain caramel (class I) is essentially burnt sugar; the other classes trade simplicity for stability in specific products.

citations.title: Mechanisms of Rebaudioside A Degradation and Ingredient-Sweetener Interactions in Beverages during Storage.
citations.abstract: The instability of rebaudioside A (Reb A) in food product applications during storage challenges their utilization. The pathways of Reb A degradation in aged acidic beverages were investigated. Three Reb A degradation compounds of known sensory importance were monitored, consisting of (1) a rearrangement, (2) a hydration, and (3) an epoxidation/rearrangement product. Using deuterium-labeled water (D2O) experiments, compounds 1-2 were reported to be generated by acid-catalyzed mechanisms involving the formation of a carbocation on carbon position 16, followed by either deprotonation via E1 elimination on C15 to form the more thermodynamically stable trisubstituted alkene (compound 1), or by the Markovnikov addition of water via SN1 substitution to form a tertiary alcohol (compound 2). Compound 3 was generated by epoxidation of the exomethylene at the C16-17 positions, followed by the opening and rearrangement of the ring to form a new alkene bond between C15-C16 and a primary alcohol on C17. Further analysis of the effect of beverage ingredients indicated the addition of caramel color significantly increased (p < 0.0001) the concentrations of compounds 1-2 compared to the aged control by 89 and 83%, respectively, whereas a specific coffee flavor and caramel color were reported to significantly reduce (p < 0.0001) the formation of compound 3 compared to the aged control during storage by 90 and 79%, respectively.

citations.title: Component of Caramel Food Coloring, THI, Causes Lymphopenia Indirectly via a Key Metabolic Intermediate.
citations.abstract: Caramel color is widely used in the food industry, and its many variations are generally considered to be safe. It has been known for a long time that THI (2-acetyl-4-(tetrahydroxybutyl)imidazole), a component of caramel color III, causes lymphopenia in animals through sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P) lyase (S1PL) inhibition. However, this mechanism of action has not been fully validated because THI does not inhibit S1PL in vitro. To reconcile this situation, we examined molecular details of THI mechanism of action using "smaller" THI derivatives. We identified a bioactive derivative, A6770, which has the same lymphopenic effect as THI via S1PL inhibition. In the case of A6770 we observe this effect both in vitro and in vivo, and demonstrate that A6770 is phosphorylated and inhibits S1PL in the same way as 4-deoxypyridoxine. In addition, A6770 was detected in rat plasma following oral administration of THI, suggesting that A6770 is a key metabolic intermediate of THI.

citations.title: Food caramels: a review.
citations.abstract: Caramel, defined as coloring agent and as an antioxidant, is being used in several kinds of food products. It has been classified into 4 classes to satisfy the requirement of several food and beverage systems. The variation in its consistency owing to its basic content of milk solids, sugars, and fat has been studied. Several methods have been found to estimate the amount of color provided by caramel in food products. Various formulations have been cited for the production of caramel by eradicating the frequent areas of problems during its processing. Caramel has been used as a synthetic colorant replacer in the baking and beverage industries. Researchers have aimed to ascertain the contribution to the antioxidant activity of some caramel-containing soft drinks. The Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives (JECFA) has established an acceptable daily intake (ADI) of Class I caramel color as "not specified"; that of Class II as 0-160 mg/kg body weight; that of Class III as 0-200 mg/kg body weight; and that of Class IV as 0-200 mg/kg body weight. This paper is an overview of the classification, physicochemical nature, formulations, coloring properties, antioxidant properties, and toxicity of caramel in different food systems.

citations.title: Caramel color safety - An update.
citations.abstract: Caramel color has been used in foods and beverages for over 150 years and is globally regulated as a color additive. The four distinct classes of caramel color (Plain Caramel, Sulfite Caramel, Ammonia Caramel, and Sulfite Ammonia Caramel) are well characterized and each have specifications that take into account processing variables including reactants that can give rise to low molecular weight constituents (e.g., 4-MeI and THI) that may have toxicological significance for evaluating safety. Extensive safety testing has been conducted with the different classes of caramel color and its constituents, including toxicokinetics, genotoxicity, subchronic toxicity, carcinogenicity, and reproductive/developmental toxicity studies. In addition, data is available on uses and use levels that have been used to estimate intakes of caramel colors and their constituents. No Observable Adverse Effect Levels (NOAEL) have been identified for all classes and Acceptable Daily Intakes have been established to ensure safety of use. Available studies support a conclusion that caramel colors are not genotoxic or carcinogenic, and exposure estimates indicate that intake of caramel colors and constituents do not pose undue safety risks. This update summarizes available relevant safety studies and authoritative reviews on caramel colors and its toxicologically important constituents, 4-MeI and THI.

citations.title: Formation of 4(5)-Methylimidazole in Aqueous d-Glucose-Amino Acids Model System.
citations.abstract: The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IRAC) has classified 4(5)-methylimidazole (4-MeI) as a group 2B possible human carcinogen. Thus, how 4-MeI forms in a D-glucose (Glu) amino acids (AA) model system is important, as it is how browning is affected. An aqueous solution of Glu was mixed individually in equimolar amounts at 3 concentrations (0.05, 0.1, and 0.15 M) with aqueous solutions of L-Alanine (Ala), L-Arginine (Arg), Glycine (Gly), L-Lysine (Lys), and L-Serine (Ser). The Glu-AA mixtures were reacted at 60, 120, and 160 °C for 1 h. The 4-MeI levels were measured by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry after derivatization with isobutylchloroformate. No 4-MeI was formed at 60 °C for any treatment combination; however, at 120 °C and 0.05 M, Glu-Arg and Glu-Lys produced 0.13 and 0.14 mg/kg of 4-MeI. At 160 °C and 0.05 M all treatment combinations formed 4-MeI. At 160 °C and 0.15 M, the observed levels of Glu-Ala, Glu-Arg, Glu-Gly, Glu-Lys, and Glu-Ser were 0.21, 1.00, 0.15, 0.22, and 0.16 mg/kg. The AA type, reactant concentrations, and temperature significantly affected (P < 0.001) formation of 4-MeI as well as browning. Glu-Lys treatment in all combinations produced the most browning, but Glu-Arg produced the most 4-MeI. This method showed that foods processed using low temperatures may have reduced levels of 4-MeI.

name: Xanthan Gum
scoreRationale: Very well tolerated at the tiny amounts used; large doses act as a laxative, and it should not be given to premature infants.
summary: Xanthan gum is a fermentation-made fiber that thickens sauces, dressings, gluten-free baking and lotions using less than 1%.

identity.composition: High-molecular-weight polysaccharide: a cellulose backbone with trisaccharide side chains of mannose and glucuronic acid.

physical.solubility: Dissolves in hot or cold water to form viscous solutions
physical.phStability: Stable from pH 2 to 12 and through heating and freezing

overview: Xanthan gum is a polysaccharide: a long, cellulose-like backbone of glucose units with a three-sugar side chain (mannose, glucuronic acid, mannose) on every second glucose. Many side chains carry acetyl and pyruvate groups, and the glucuronic acid carries a negative charge.

In water, the side chains wrap around the backbone and stiffen it into a rod-like helix. Rigid rods tangle and trap water, so less than 1% xanthan can turn a thin liquid into a thick, pourable sauce, and it works whether the liquid is hot, cold, salty or acidic.
profile.function: Creates viscosity and suspends particles, keeping dressings from separating and replacing gluten's structure in gluten-free baking.

mechanisms.title: Shear thinning
mechanisms.chemical: Under stirring, squeezing or chewing, the rod-like chains align with the flow and slide past each other, so viscosity drops; at rest they tangle again.
mechanisms.biological: That's why a dressing pours easily from the bottle but clings to lettuce, and why toothpaste stays on the brush. In the mouth, the sauce feels smooth rather than gummy.

mechanisms.title: Helping people swallow safely
mechanisms.chemical: Thickened liquids flow more slowly and hold together as one cohesive mouthful.
mechanisms.biological: Speech therapists thicken drinks with xanthan for people with dysphagia (difficulty swallowing), which lowers the risk of liquid slipping into the airway.

mechanisms.title: A fermentable fiber
mechanisms.chemical: Human digestive enzymes can't break xanthan's β-glycosidic bonds, but some colon bacteria can.
mechanisms.biological: It adds bulk and is partly fermented into short-chain fatty acids. Large amounts (above about 15 g a day) act as a laxative.

reactions.title: Gelling with locust bean gum
reactions.summary: Two gums that don't gel alone form an elastic gel together.

steps.name: Helix
steps.text: Xanthan forms stiff helices in solution.

steps.name: Binding
steps.text: Smooth, unbranched regions of locust bean gum's galactomannan chains bind along the xanthan helices.

steps.name: Network
steps.text: These junction zones link many chains into an elastic, three-dimensional gel.

reactions.result: This synergy is used in some desserts, pet foods and gluten-free products.

reactions.title: Precipitation with alcohol (purification)
reactions.summary: Changing the solvent pulls xanthan out of the fermentation broth.

steps.name: Pasteurize
steps.text: The broth is heated to kill the bacteria.

steps.name: Lower polarity
steps.text: Isopropyl alcohol is added, making the liquid less able to hydrate the gum.

steps.name: Aggregate
steps.text: Xanthan chains lose their water shells, clump into fibers, and are filtered, dried and milled.

reactions.result: The alcohol is recovered and reused; finished xanthan contains only trace residues.

regulatory.status: Approved food additive.
ADI "not specified"; FDA and EFSA advise against use in premature infants after thickener-associated necrotizing enterocolitis cases.

hazards.title: Not for premature infants
hazards.summary: Safe for older children and adults, but avoided in preemies.
hazards.chemical: Gut bacteria ferment xanthan, producing gas and acids.
hazards.biological: FDA warned in 2011 after cases of necrotizing enterocolitis (a serious bowel condition) in premature babies fed a xanthan-based thickener.

hazards.title: Digestive effects at high doses
hazards.summary: Typical food amounts are tiny.
hazards.chemical: Undigested gum holds water and is fermented in the colon.
hazards.biological: Very large amounts cause bloating, gas and loose stools.

profile.dosage: Foods use about 0.05–0.5%. Laxative effects appear above about 15 g/day.

myths.claim: Xanthan gum is made from bacteria, so it's unsafe.
myths.consensus: Bacteria make it during fermentation, but the purified gum contains no living organisms.

synthesis.title: Bacterial fermentation
synthesis.summary: A plant bacterium makes xanthan as protective slime.
synthesis.mechanism: Xanthomonas campestris is grown in a sugar solution and secretes xanthan around its cells. After fermentation, the broth is pasteurized, the gum is precipitated with isopropyl alcohol, then dried and milled into powder.
synthesis.significance: The same bacterium causes black rot on cabbage; its slime helps it cling to leaves.

citations.title: What makes Xanthomonas albilineans unique amongst xanthomonads?
citations.abstract: Xanthomonas albilineans causes leaf scald, a lethal disease of sugarcane. Compared to other species of Xanthomonas, X. albilineans exhibits distinctive pathogenic mechanisms, ecology and taxonomy. Its genome, which has experienced significant erosion, has unique genomic features. It lacks two loci required for pathogenicity in other plant pathogenic species of Xanthomonas: the xanthan gum biosynthesis and the Hrp-T3SS (hypersensitive response and pathogenicity-type three secretion system) gene clusters. Instead, X. albilineans harbors in its genome an SPI-1 (Salmonella pathogenicity island-1) T3SS gene cluster usually found in animal pathogens. X. albilineans produces a potent DNA gyrase inhibitor called albicidin, which blocks chloroplast differentiation, resulting in the characteristic white foliar stripe symptoms. The antibacterial activity of albicidin also confers on X. albilineans a competitive advantage against rival bacteria during sugarcane colonization. Recent chemical studies have uncovered the unique structure of albicidin and allowed us to partially elucidate its fascinating biosynthesis apparatus, which involves an enigmatic hybrid PKS/NRPS (polyketide synthase/non-ribosomal peptide synthetase) machinery.

citations.title: Natural Regenerative Hydrogels for Wound Healing.
citations.authors: Chelu, Calderon Moreno, Musuc et al.
citations.abstract: Regenerative hydrogels from natural polymers have come forth as auspicious materials for use in regenerative medicine, with interest attributed to their intrinsic biodegradability, biocompatibility, and ability to reassemble the extracellular matrix. This review covers the latest advances in regenerative hydrogels used for wound healing, focusing on their chemical composition, cross-linking mechanisms, and functional properties. Key carbohydrate polymers, including alginate, chitosan, hyaluronic acid, and polysaccharide gums, including agarose, carrageenan, and xanthan gum, are discussed in terms of their sources, chemical structures and specific properties suitable for regenerative applications. The review further explores the categorization of hydrogels based on ionic charge, response to physiological stimuli (i.e., pH, temperature) and particularized roles in wound tissue self-healing. Various methods of cross-linking used to enhance the mechanical and biological performance of these hydrogels are also examined. By highlighting recent innovations and ongoing challenges, this article intends to give a detailed understanding of natural hydrogels and their potential to revolutionize regenerative medicine and improve patient healing outcomes.

citations.title: Recent trends on gellan gum blends with natural and synthetic polymers: A review.
citations.abstract: Gellan gum (GG), a linear negatively charged exopolysaccharide,is biodegradable and non-toxic in nature. It produces hard and translucent gel in the presence of metallic ions which is stable at low pH. However, GG has poor mechanical strength, poor stability in physiological conditions, high gelling temperature and small temperature window.Therefore,it is blended with different polymers such as agar, chitosan, cellulose, sodium alginate, starch, pectin, polyanaline, pullulan, polyvinyl chloride, and xanthan gum. In this article, a comprehensive overview of combination of GG with natural and synthetic polymers/compounds and their applications in biomedical field involving drug delivery system, insulin delivery, wound healing and gene therapy, is presented. It also describes the utilization of GG based materials in food and petroleum industry. All the technical scientific issues have been addressed; highlighting the recent advancement.

citations.title: Polysaccharide-based nanofibers for pharmaceutical and biomedical applications: A review.
citations.authors: Priya, Batra, R N et al.
citations.abstract: Nanofibers are fibrous nanocarriers that can be synthesized from natural polymers, synthetic polymers, semiconducting materials, composite materials, and carbon-based materials. Recently, natural polysaccharides-based nanofibers are gaining attention in the field of pharmaceuticals and biomedical as these are biocompatible, biodegradable, non-toxic, and economic. Nanofibers can deliver a significant amount of drug to the targeted site and provide effective interaction of therapeutic agent at the site of action due to a larger surface area. Other important advantages of nanofibers are low density, high porosity, small pore size, high mechanical strength, and low cost. In this review, natural polysaccharides such as alginate, pullulan, hyaluronic acid, dextran, cellulose, chondroitin sulfate, chitosan, xanthan gum, and gellan gum are discussed for their characteristics, pharmaceutical utility, and biomedical applications. The authors have given particular emphasis to the several fabrication processes that utilize these polysaccharides to form nanofibers, and their recent updates in pharmaceutical applications such as drug delivery, tissue engineering, skin disorders, wound-healing dressings, cancer therapy, bioactive molecules delivery, anti-infectives, and solubility enhancement. Despite these many advantages, nanofibers have been explored less for their scale-up and applications in advanced therapeutic delivery.

citations.title: Xanthan gum in drug release.
citations.abstract: Controlled release is of vital relevance for many drugs; thus, there is a keen interest in materials that can improve the release profiles of formulations administered via buccal, transdermal, ophthalmic, vaginal, and nasal. The desirable effects of those materials include the improvement of stability, adhesiveness, solubility, and retention time. Hence, different synthetic and natural polymers are utilized to achieve these objectives. In this respect, xanthan gum is an anionic polysaccharide that can be obtained from Xanthomonas bacteria. It is a natural polymer broadly employed in numerous food products, lotions, shampoos, and dermatological articles. Furthermore, due to its physicochemical features, xanthan gum is growingly utilized for the development and improvement of drug delivery systems. In this regard, encouraging findings have been revealed by recent formulations for pharmaceutical applications, including antiviral carriers, antibacterial transporters, transdermal patches, vaginal formulations, and anticancer medications. In this article, we perform a concise description of the chemical properties of xanthan gum and its role as a modifier of drug release. Furthermore, we present an outlook of the state of the art of research focused on the utilization of xanthan gum in varied pharmaceutical formulations, which include tablets, films, hydrogels, and nanoformulations. Finally, we discuss some perspectives about the use of xanthan gum in these formulations.

name: Soy Lecithin
scoreRationale: A natural phospholipid mixture with a long safety record; trace soy protein matters only for highly sensitive allergy sufferers.
summary: Lecithin is a natural emulsifier from soybean oil that helps oil and water mix in chocolate, dressings and creams.

identity.composition: Mixture of phospholipids (phosphatidylcholine, phosphatidylethanolamine, phosphatidylinositol), glycolipids and triglycerides.

physical.solubility: Disperses in water; soluble in oils

overview: Lecithin is a mixture of phospholipids, chiefly phosphatidylcholine. Each phospholipid has a glycerol backbone carrying two fatty-acid tails, which repel water, and a phosphate group linked to a small charged molecule such as choline, which loves water.
That two-faced (amphiphilic) structure is the same design as the phospholipids in every cell membrane. It lets lecithin sit at the boundary between oil and water and hold the two together.
profile.function: Stabilizes emulsions, reduces chocolate viscosity, prevents sticking in cooking sprays and softens skin in creams.

mechanisms.title: Emulsifying oil and water
mechanisms.chemical: Lecithin molecules line up at oil–water boundaries with their tails in the oil and their heads in the water, lowering the tension between the two and coating each droplet.
mechanisms.biological: Coated droplets repel one another instead of merging, so dressings, margarine and chocolate stay smooth; on the tongue the product melts and spreads evenly.

mechanisms.title: A source of choline
mechanisms.chemical: Digestive enzymes break phosphatidylcholine apart, releasing choline.
mechanisms.biological: Choline is needed to build cell membranes and to make the neurotransmitter acetylcholine; eggs and soy are major dietary sources.

mechanisms.title: Helping absorb dietary fat
mechanisms.chemical: Pancreatic phospholipase A2 removes one fatty acid, forming lysophosphatidylcholine, an even stronger emulsifier.
mechanisms.biological: It helps form the tiny micelles that carry fats and fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) into intestinal cells.

reactions.title: Forming an emulsion
reactions.summary: Lecithin stabilizes droplets of one liquid inside another.

steps.name: Orientation
steps.text: Molecules migrate to the oil–water boundary, tails into oil, heads into water.

steps.name: Coating
steps.text: A single layer of lecithin wraps each droplet.

steps.name: Stabilizing
steps.text: Charged heads make droplets repel each other, preventing them from merging.

reactions.result: Mayonnaise works the same way using lecithin from egg yolk.

reactions.title: Enzymatic modification
reactions.summary: Food technologists can tune lecithin with enzymes.

steps.name: Hydrolysis
steps.text: Phospholipase enzymes cut one fatty acid from each phospholipid.

steps.name: Product
steps.text: The result, lysolecithin, has one tail instead of two.

steps.name: Effect
steps.text: With a smaller tail, it prefers oil-in-water emulsions and works better in baked goods.

reactions.result: Changing a molecule's shape changes which kind of emulsion it stabilizes.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe.
ADI "not specified"; no safety concern at reported uses.
Declared as soy under FALCPA because trace soy protein may remain.

hazards.title: Trace soy protein
hazards.summary: Matters only for highly sensitive soy-allergic people.
hazards.chemical: Refining removes most soy protein, but traces can remain.
hazards.biological: Most people with soy allergy tolerate lecithin; U.S. labels still declare it as soy.

profile.dosage: Chocolate uses about 0.3–0.5%. Supplement doses of several grams per day are well tolerated.

myths.claim: Soy lecithin disrupts hormones.
myths.consensus: Lecithin contains negligible isoflavones; the phytoestrogen debate concerns whole soy foods and supplements.

synthesis.title: Degumming soybean oil
synthesis.summary: Lecithin is a byproduct of making clear cooking oil.
synthesis.mechanism: Crude soybean oil is mixed with a little water. The phospholipids absorb water, swell into a sticky gum and separate from the oil. Centrifuges spin out the gum, which is dried into lecithin.
synthesis.significance: Removing the gums keeps the oil from turning cloudy, and the gums become a useful product.

synthesis.title: Biological synthesis
synthesis.summary: Every plant and animal cell makes phosphatidylcholine.
synthesis.mechanism: In the Kennedy pathway, choline is phosphorylated, activated as CDP-choline, then attached to a diacylglycerol molecule to form phosphatidylcholine.
synthesis.significance: Lecithin was first isolated from egg yolk in the 1840s; its name comes from the Greek lekithos, meaning yolk.

citations.title: Lecithin cholesterol acyltransferase.
citations.abstract: Cholesterol transport in circulation and its removal from tissues depends on the activity of lecithin cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT). LCAT is a soluble enzyme that converts cholesterol and phosphatidylcholines (lecithins) to cholesteryl esters and lyso-phosphatidylcholines on the surface of high-density lipoproteins. This review presents key background information and recent research advances on the structure of human LCAT, its reactions and substrates, and the expression of the LCAT gene. While the three-dimensional structure of LCAT is not yet known, a partial model now exists that facilitates the study of structure-function relationships of the native enzyme, and of natural and engineered mutants. The LCAT reaction on lipoproteins consists of several steps, starting with enzyme binding to the lipoprotein/lipid surface, followed by activation of LCAT by apolipoproteins, binding of lipid substrates and the catalytic steps giving rise to the lipid products. Quantitative data are presented on the kinetic and equilibrium constants of some of the LCAT reaction steps. Finally, overexpression of the human LCAT gene in mice and rabbits has been used to examine the physiologic role of LCAT in vivo and its protective effect against diet induced atherosclerosis.

citations.title: Lecithin:cholesterol acyltransferase: old friend or foe in atherosclerosis?
citations.abstract: Lecithin:cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT) is a key enzyme that catalyzes the esterification of free cholesterol in plasma lipoproteins and plays a critical role in high-density lipoprotein (HDL) metabolism. Deficiency leads to accumulation of nascent preβ-HDL due to impaired maturation of HDL particles, whereas enhanced expression is associated with the formation of large, apoE-rich HDL(1) particles. In addition to its function in HDL metabolism, LCAT was believed to be an important driving force behind macrophage reverse cholesterol transport (RCT) and, therefore, has been a subject of great interest in cardiovascular research since its discovery in 1962. Although half a century has passed, the importance of LCAT for atheroprotection is still under intense debate. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the insights that have been gained in the past 50 years on the biochemistry of LCAT, the role of LCAT in lipoprotein metabolism and the pathogenesis of atherosclerosis in animal models, and its impact on cardiovascular disease in humans.

citations.title: Multi-liposomal containers.
citations.abstract: Small unilamellar liposomes, 40-60 nm in diameter, composed of anionic diphosphatidylglycerol (cardiolipin, CL(2-)) or phosphatidylcerine (PS(1-)) and zwitter-ionic egg yolk lecithin (EL) or dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC), electrostatically complex with polystyrene microspheres, ca. 100 nm in diameter, grafted by polycationic chains ("spherical polycationic brushes", SPBs). Polymer/liposome binding studies were carried out using electrophoretic mobility (EPM), dynamic light scattering (DLS), fluorescence, conductometry, differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), and cryogenic transmission electron microscopy (cryo-TEM) as the main analytical tools. By these means a remarkably detailed picture emerges of molecular events inside a membrane. The following are among the most important conclusions that arose from the experiments: (a) binding of liposomes to SPBs is accompanied by flip-flop of anionic lipids from the inner to the outer leaflet of the liposomal membrane along with lateral lipid segregation into "islands". (b) The SPB-induced structural reorganization of the liposomal membrane, together with the geometry of anionic lipid molecules, determines the maximum molar fraction of anionic lipid (a key parameter designated as ν) that ensures the structural integrity of liposomes upon complexation: ν=0.3 for liposomes with conically-shaped CL(2-) and ν=0.5 for liposomes with anionic cylindrically-shaped PS(1-). (c) The number of intact liposomes per SPB particle varies from 40 for (ν=0.1) to 13 (ν=0.5). (d) By using a mixture of liposomes with variety of encapsulated substances, multi-liposomal complexes can be prepared with a high loading capacity and a controlled ratio of the contents. (e) In order to make the mixed anionic liposomes pH-sensitive, they are additionally modified by 30 mol% of a morpholinocyclohexanol-based lipid that undergoes a conformational flip when changing pH. Being complexed with SPBs, such liposomes rapidly release their contents when the pH is reduced from 7.0 to 5.0. The results allow loaded liposomes to be concentrated within a rather small volume and, thereby, the preparation of multi-liposomal containers of promise in the drug delivery field.

citations.title: Functions of Intracellular Retinoid Binding-Proteins.
citations.abstract: Multiple binding and transport proteins facilitate many aspects of retinoid biology through effects on retinoid transport, cellular uptake, metabolism, and nuclear delivery. These include the serum retinol binding protein sRBP (aka Rbp4), the plasma membrane sRBP receptor Stra6, and the intracellular retinoid binding-proteins such as cellular retinol-binding proteins (CRBP) and cellular retinoic acid binding-proteins (CRABP). sRBP transports the highly lipophilic retinol through an aqueous medium. The major intracellular retinol-binding protein, CRBP1, likely enhances efficient retinoid use by providing a sink to facilitate retinol uptake from sRBP through the plasma membrane or via Stra6, delivering retinol or retinal to select enzymes that generate retinyl esters or retinoic acid, and protecting retinol/retinal from excess catabolism or opportunistic metabolism. Intracellular retinoic acid binding-proteins (CRABP1 and 2, and FABP5) seem to have more diverse functions distinctive to each, such as directing retinoic acid to catabolism, delivering retinoic acid to specific nuclear receptors, and generating non-canonical actions. Gene ablation of intracellular retinoid binding-proteins does not cause embryonic lethality or gross morphological defects. Metabolic and functional defects manifested in knockouts of CRBP1, CRBP2 and CRBP3, however, illustrate their essentiality to health, and in the case of CRBP2, to survival during limited dietary vitamin A. Future studies should continue to address the specific molecular interactions that occur between retinoid binding-proteins and their targets and their precise physiologic contributions to retinoid homeostasis and function.

citations.title: Myeloperoxidase: an oxidative pathway for generating dysfunctional high-density lipoprotein.
citations.abstract: Accumulation of low-density lipoprotein (LDL)-derived cholesterol by artery wall macrophages triggers atherosclerosis, the leading cause of cardiovascular disease. Conversely, high-density lipoprotein (HDL) retards atherosclerosis by promoting cholesterol efflux from macrophages by the membrane-associated ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1) pathway. HDL has been proposed to lose its cardioprotective effects in subjects with atherosclerosis, but the underlying mechanisms are poorly understood. One potential pathway involves oxidative damage by myeloperoxidase (MPO), a heme enzyme secreted by human artery wall macrophages. We used mass spectrometry to demonstrate that HDL isolated from patients with established cardiovascular disease contains elevated levels of 3-chlorotyrosine and 3-nitrotyrosine, two characteristic products of MPO. When apolipoprotein A-I (apoA-I), the major HDL protein, was oxidized by MPO, its ability to promote cellular cholesterol efflux by ABCA1 was impaired. Moreover, oxidized apoA-I was unable to activate lecithin:cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT), which rapidly converts free cholesterol to cholesteryl ester, a critical step in HDL maturation. Biochemical studies implicated tyrosine chlorination and methionine oxygenation in the loss of ABCA1 and LCAT activity by oxidized apoA-I. Oxidation of specific residues in apoA-I inhibited two key steps in cholesterol efflux from macrophages, raising the possibility that MPO initiates a pathway for generating dysfunctional HDL in humans.

name: Sodium Bicarbonate
scoreRationale: Extremely safe at normal uses; only large ingestions (as a home antacid) pose risks.
summary: Baking soda leavens baked goods, neutralizes odors, and scrubs gently. It's one of the safest multi-purpose household chemicals.

overview: Sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO₃) is made of sodium ions and bicarbonate ions (HCO₃⁻). Bicarbonate is amphoteric: it can accept a proton to become carbonic acid or give one up to become carbonate, so it neutralizes acids and resists strong bases.
When bicarbonate meets an acid, it releases carbon dioxide gas, the bubbles that make pancakes and cakes rise. The very same bicarbonate ion is the main pH buffer in your blood.
profile.function: Releases CO2 to raise dough, neutralizes acids and odors, softens water, and acts as a mild abrasive in toothpaste and cleaners.

mechanisms.title: Buffering blood pH
mechanisms.chemical: In blood, the enzyme carbonic anhydrase rapidly converts CO₂ and water into carbonic acid, which splits into H⁺ and HCO₃⁻, and back again.
mechanisms.biological: Lungs adjust how much CO₂ you exhale and kidneys adjust bicarbonate, keeping blood pH between 7.35 and 7.45. Doctors give intravenous bicarbonate to correct severe acidosis.

mechanisms.title: Antacid
mechanisms.chemical: Bicarbonate neutralizes hydrochloric acid in the stomach, producing salt, water and carbon dioxide.
mechanisms.biological: Heartburn eases within minutes; the released CO₂ is why people often burp afterward.

mechanisms.title: Neutralizing odors
mechanisms.chemical: Many unpleasant smells are acids (such as butyric acid in sour milk); bicarbonate converts them into non-volatile salts.
mechanisms.biological: Molecules that can't evaporate can't reach the smell receptors in your nose, so the odor fades.

reactions.title: Leavening with acid
reactions.summary: Acid plus baking soda makes gas bubbles.

steps.name: Proton transfer
steps.text: An acid in the batter (buttermilk, yogurt, or the acid salt in baking powder) donates H⁺ to bicarbonate.

steps.name: Carbonic acid
steps.text: Bicarbonate becomes carbonic acid, which is unstable.

steps.name: Gas
steps.text: Carbonic acid breaks into water and carbon dioxide, which inflates bubbles that expand further in the oven's heat.

reactions.result: Baking powder packages baking soda with a dry acid, so it only needs water and heat to work.

reactions.title: Thermal decomposition
reactions.summary: Heat alone breaks baking soda down.

steps.name: Heating
steps.text: Above about 80 °C, bicarbonate ions begin to react with each other.

steps.name: Release
steps.text: Pairs of bicarbonate ions form carbonate, water and carbon dioxide.

steps.name: Residue
steps.text: Sodium carbonate is left behind.

reactions.result: Too much baking soda without enough acid leaves sodium carbonate, which tastes soapy and bitter.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe.
Authorized as E500(ii) at quantum satis.
Safe as used in cosmetics.

hazards.title: Large ingestions
hazards.summary: A risk when people overuse it as a home antacid.
hazards.chemical: Excess bicarbonate overwhelms the body's buffering, raising blood pH (metabolic alkalosis) and sodium levels.
hazards.biological: Symptoms include muscle twitching and confusion. Rapid CO₂ release after a large meal has, rarely, ruptured the stomach.

profile.dosage: Baking uses about 1 teaspoon per recipe. Antacid labels limit adult use to a few grams per day.

myths.claim: Baking soda plus vinegar is a super cleaner.
myths.consensus: They neutralize each other into salty water; the fizz is only CO2. Each works better on its own.

myths.claim: Baking soda cures cancer by alkalizing the body.
myths.consensus: Blood pH is tightly regulated; diet cannot meaningfully change it, and this claim has caused harm.

environment.persistence: Not persistent; part of the natural carbonate cycle.

synthesis.title: The Solvay process
synthesis.summary: Made from salt, limestone and ammonia.
synthesis.mechanism: Brine is saturated with ammonia, then carbon dioxide is bubbled through. Sodium bicarbonate, the least soluble product, crystallizes out and is filtered off; the ammonia is recovered and reused.
synthesis.equation: NaCl + NH3 + CO2 + H2O → NaHCO3 + NH4Cl
synthesis.significance: Ernest Solvay's 1860s process made soda chemicals cheap enough for everyday use.

synthesis.title: From trona ore
synthesis.summary: Much U.S. baking soda starts as a mineral.
synthesis.mechanism: Trona, mined in Wyoming's Green River Basin, is refined into sodium carbonate, which is then dissolved and reacted with carbon dioxide to form sodium bicarbonate.

citations.title: Pancreatic enzyme supplementation for patients receiving enteral feeds.
citations.abstract: Background: Pancreatic enzyme supplementation is an important part of management for a number of gastrointestinal conditions. For patients who are unable to swallow pancreatin capsules or granules, enteral feeding tubes can be used to administer the pancreatic enzyme. This presents challenges given the unique format of the pancreatic enzyme supplements, with common problems including tube blockage and loss of the enzyme's effect. Methods and results: A novel technique is described for administration of pancreatic enzyme via feeding tubes. For gastrically placed tubes, this involves opening the pancreatin capsules and suspending the enzyme microspheres in thickened acidic fluid (such as the mildly thickened or "nectar-thick" fruit juice used for dysphagia) for delivery into the feeding tube. This technique minimizes tube blockage by preventing the enzyme from clumping in the tube. For jejunally placed tubes, enzyme microspheres can be crushed and activated with sodium bicarbonate before flushing into the tube, or the activated enzyme mixture can be added to enteral feeds. Conclusions: Pancreatic enzyme supplementation can continue while patients receive enteral feeding. Using the described technique can help to avoid tube blockage and maintain optimal enzyme activity.

citations.title: Rhabdomyolysis.
citations.abstract: Rhabdomyolysis is a syndrome involving the breakdown of skeletal muscle causing myoglobin and other intracellular proteins and electrolytes to leak into the circulation. The development of rhabdomyolysis is associated with a wide variety of diseases, injuries, medications and toxins. While the exact mechanisms responsible for all the causes are not fully understood, it is clear that muscle damage can occur from direct injury or by metabolic inequalities between energy consumption and energy production. Rhabdomyolysis is diagnosed by elevations in serum creatine phosphokinase (CPK), and while there is no established serum level cut-off, many clinicians use five times the upper limit of normal ( approximately 1000 U/l). Rhabdomyolysis can be complicated by acute renal failure (occurring in 4%-33% of patients), compartment syndrome, cardiac dysrhythmias via electrolyte abnormalities, and disseminated intravascular coagulopathy. The mainstay of treatment is hospitalisation with aggressive intravenous fluid (IVF) resuscitation with the correction/prevention of electrolyte abnormalities. There are additional adjunctive therapies to IVF, such as alkalinisation of the urine with sodium bicarbonate, diuretic therapy or combinations of both; however the lack of large randomised control studies concerning the benefits of these treatments makes it difficult to make strong recommendations for or against their use in the treatment of rhabdomyolysis. Regardless of these controversies, the overall prognosis for rhabdomyolysis is favourable when treated with early and aggressive IVF resuscitation, and full recovery of renal function is common. Irrespective of the cause of rhabdomyolysis the mortality rate may still be as high as 8%. This is a comprehensive review of the pathophysiology, diagnosis, complications and treatment options for rhabdomyolysis.

citations.title: Complexities, Benefits, Risks, and Clinical Implications of Sodium Bicarbonate Administration in Critically Ill Patients: A State-of-the-Art Review.
citations.abstract: Sodium bicarbonate has been used in the treatment of different pathologies, such as hyperkalemia, cardiac arrest, tricyclic antidepressant toxicity, aspirin toxicity, acute acidosis, lactic acidosis, diabetic ketoacidosis, rhabdomyolysis, and adrenergic receptors' resistance to catecholamine in patients with shock. An ongoing debate about bicarbonate's efficacy and potential harm has been raised for decades because of the lack of evidence supporting its potential efficacy. Despite the guidelines' restrictions, sodium bicarbonate has been overused in clinical practice. The overuse of sodium bicarbonate could be because of the desire to correct the arterial blood gas parameters rapidly instead of achieving homeostasis by treating the cause of the metabolic acidosis. Moreover, it is believed that sodium bicarbonate may reverse acidosis-induced myocardial depression, hemodynamic instability, ventricular arrhythmias, impaired cellular energy production, resistance to catecholamines, altered metabolism, enzyme suppression, immune dysfunction, and ineffective oxygen delivery. On the other hand, it is crucial to pay attention to the potential harm that could be caused by excessive sodium bicarbonate administration. Sodium bicarbonate may cause paradoxical respiratory acidosis, intracellular acidosis, hypokalemia, hypocalcemia, alkalosis, impaired oxygen delivery, cerebrospinal fluid acidosis, and neurologic dysfunction. In this review, we discuss the pathophysiology of sodium bicarbonate-induced adverse effects and potential benefits. We also review the most recent clinical trials, observational studies, and guidelines discussing the use of sodium bicarbonate in different pathologies. Sodium bicarbonate is a multifaceted medication that plays a crucial role in managing and treating diverse disease pathologies. This activity delves into the expansive applications of sodium bicarbonate, providing healthcare professionals with a nuanced understanding of its indications, mechanism of action, and contraindications. The program focuses on its pivotal role in treating conditions such as lactic acidosis and QRS prolongation, offering participants in-depth insights into therapeutic considerations, including dosing, toxicities, and relevant interactions. By examining sodium bicarbonate's adverse event profile, participants will be better equipped to ensure its effective utilization across a spectrum of clinical scenarios. This evidence-based activity aims to empower interprofessional healthcare team members with the essential knowledge to optimize sodium bicarbonate's potential to enhance patient outcomes.

citations.title: Perioperative Clinical Trials in AKI.
citations.abstract: To characterize current evidence and current foci of perioperative clinical trials, we systematically reviewed Medline and identified perioperative trials involving 100 or more adult patients undergoing surgery and reporting renal end points that were published in high-impact journals since 2004. We categorized the 101 trials identified based on the nature of the intervention and summarized major trial findings from the five categories most applicable to perioperative management of patients. Trials that targeted ischemia suggested that increasing perioperative renal oxygen delivery with inotropes or blood transfusion does not reliably mitigate acute kidney injury (AKI), although goal-directed therapy with hemodynamic monitors appeared beneficial in some trials. Trials that have targeted inflammation or oxidative stress, including studies of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, steroids, N-acetylcysteine, and sodium bicarbonate, have not shown renal benefits, and high-dose perioperative statin treatment increased AKI in some patient groups in two large trials. Balanced crystalloid intravenous fluids appear safer than saline, and crystalloids appear safer than colloids. Liberal compared with restrictive fluid administration reduced AKI in a recent large trial in open abdominal surgery. Remote ischemic preconditioning, although effective in several smaller trials, failed to reduce AKI in two larger trials. The translation of promising preclinical therapies to patients undergoing surgery remains poor, and most interventions that reduced perioperative AKI compared novel surgical management techniques or existing processes of care rather than novel pharmacologic interventions.

citations.title: Methanol poisoning.
citations.abstract: Methanol ingestion is an uncommon form of poisoning that can cause severe metabolic disturbances, blindness, permanent neurologic dysfunction and death. While methanol itself may be harmless, it is converted in vivo to the highly toxic formic acid. The diagnosis is sometimes elusive and requires a high index of suspicion. Because antidotal treatment is available it is important to recognize methanol poisoning promptly. The presence of metabolic acidosis associated with an increased anion gap and increased osmol gap are important laboratory findings. Specific therapeutic measures include correction of the metabolic acidosis with sodium bicarbonate and administration of enteral or parenteral ethanol to competitively inhibit the metabolic breakdown of methanol to formic acid. Hemodialysis accelerates the elimination of both methanol and formic acid and also assists in correction of the metabolic acidosis. Experimental data suggests that administration of folic acid may be of benefit by hastening the metabolism of formic acid to carbon dioxide. Prompt institution of specific therapy can probably decrease the morbidity and mortality associated with this form of poisoning.
