name: Vinegar
scoreRationale: Household vinegar is low hazard and biodegradable; concentrated acetic acid is corrosive.
summary: Vinegar (dilute acetic acid) dissolves mineral scale, cuts soap scum and flavors food. It's one of the gentlest cleaners.

physical.state: Clear liquid (5% in table vinegar, 6–10% in cleaning vinegar)

overview: Acetic acid (CH₃COOH) is a two-carbon carboxylic acid: a methyl group attached to a –COOH group. It's a weak acid (pKa 4.76), so in vinegar, which is about 5% acetic acid, only a small fraction of molecules release their proton at any moment.

Pure acetic acid freezes at 16.6 °C into ice-like crystals, which is why it's called glacial acetic acid. Vinegar's sharp smell is acetic acid evaporating; its cleaning power comes from dissolving the alkaline mineral deposits left by hard water.
profile.function: Dissolves limescale and soap scum, deodorizes, and adds sourness and preservation to foods.

mechanisms.title: Dissolving limescale
mechanisms.chemical: Acetic acid reacts with calcium carbonate deposits, converting them into soluble calcium acetate and carbon dioxide.
mechanisms.biological: Kettle scale, faucet crust and soap scum loosen and rinse away.

mechanisms.title: Preserving food
mechanisms.chemical: Uncharged acetic acid crosses microbial membranes, then releases its proton inside the cell, acidifying it.
mechanisms.biological: Spoilage and disease-causing bacteria can't grow in pickles and other vinegar-preserved foods.

mechanisms.title: Blood sugar after meals
mechanisms.chemical: Acetic acid may slow stomach emptying and inhibit sugar-digesting enzymes in the gut.
mechanisms.biological: Small trials found a tablespoon or two of vinegar with a meal modestly lowers the rise in blood sugar afterward.

reactions.title: Dissolving limescale
reactions.summary: Acid meets carbonate.

steps.name: Proton transfer
steps.text: Acetic acid donates protons to carbonate in the scale.

steps.name: Carbonic acid
steps.text: Carbonic acid forms and breaks down into water and carbon dioxide (the fizz).

steps.name: Soluble salt
steps.text: Calcium is left as dissolved calcium acetate.

reactions.result: Soaking a showerhead in vinegar overnight uses exactly this reaction.

reactions.title: Acetic fermentation
reactions.summary: How wine becomes vinegar.

steps.name: Bacteria
steps.text: Acetobacter bacteria live at the surface of alcoholic liquids, where there's oxygen.

steps.name: Oxidation
steps.text: They oxidize ethanol to acetaldehyde, then to acetic acid.

steps.name: Mother of vinegar
steps.text: A slimy cellulose mat of bacteria (the “mother”) forms on the surface.

reactions.result: The French “vin aigre” means sour wine.

regulatory.status: Generally Recognized as Safe.
Vinegar is not a registered disinfectant for germ-kill claims.
Concentrated acetic acid: causes severe skin burns (H314) and is flammable.

hazards.title: Concentrated acid is corrosive
hazards.summary: Household vinegar is safe; 20–30% horticultural vinegar is not.
hazards.chemical: Concentrated acetic acid denatures proteins and burns tissue.
hazards.biological: Strong cleaning or weed-killing vinegars require gloves and eye protection.

hazards.title: Never mix with bleach
hazards.summary: Vinegar is an acid.
hazards.chemical: Adding acid to bleach releases chlorine gas.
hazards.biological: Chlorine gas irritates and damages the lungs.

profile.dosage: Table vinegar at 5% is safe to eat; 20–30% "horticultural vinegar" requires protective gear.

myths.claim: Vinegar disinfects as well as bleach.
myths.consensus: It reduces some bacteria but doesn't reliably kill many pathogens; use a registered disinfectant when needed.

myths.claim: Vinegar is safe on every surface.
myths.consensus: Its acid can etch marble, granite and some finishes.

synthesis.title: Bacterial fermentation (vinegar)
synthesis.summary: How food vinegar is made.
synthesis.mechanism: Alcohol from fermented fruit, grain or rice is oxidized by Acetobacter bacteria in tanks with vigorous aeration until it reaches about 5% acetic acid.

synthesis.title: Methanol carbonylation (industrial acid)
synthesis.summary: How most acetic acid for chemicals is made.
synthesis.mechanism: Methanol and carbon monoxide react over a rhodium or iridium catalyst with an iodide promoter (the Monsanto and Cativa processes).
synthesis.significance: Industrial acetic acid goes into vinyl acetate for paints and glues, and into PET plastic.

citations.title: New developments in oxidative fermentation.
citations.abstract: Oxidative fermentations have been well established for a long time, especially in vinegar and in L-sorbose production. Recently, information on the enzyme systems involved in these oxidative fermentations has accumulated and new developments are possible based on these findings. We have recently isolated several thermotolerant acetic acid bacteria, which also seem to be useful for new developments in oxidative fermentation. Two different types of membrane-bound enzymes, quinoproteins and flavoproteins, are involved in oxidative fermentation, and sometimes work with the same substrate but produce different oxidation products. Recently, there have been new developments in two different oxidative fermentations, D-gluconate and D-sorbitol oxidations. Flavoproteins, D-gluconate dehydrogenase, and D-sorbitol dehydrogenase were isolated almost 2 decades ago, while the enzyme involved in the same oxidation reaction for D-gluconate and D-sorbitol has been recently isolated and shown to be a quinoprotein. Thus, these flavoproteins and a quinoprotein have been re-assessed for the oxidation reaction. Flavoprotein D-gluconate dehydrogenase and D-sorbitol dehydrogenase were shown to produce 2-keto- D-gluconate and D-fructose, respectively, whereas the quinoprotein was shown to produce 5-keto- D-gluconate and L-sorbose from D-gluconate and D-sorbitol, respectively. In addition to the quinoproteins described above, a new quinoprotein for quinate oxidation has been recently isolated from Gluconobacter strains. The quinate dehydrogenase is also a membrane-bound quinoprotein that produces 3-dehydroquinate. This enzyme can be useful for the production of shikimate, which is a convenient salvage synthesis system for many antibiotics, herbicides, and aromatic amino acids synthesis. In order to reduce energy costs of oxidative fermentation in industry, several thermotolerant acetic acid bacteria that can grow up to 40 degrees C have been isolated. Of such isolated strains, some thermotolerant Acetobacter species were found to be useful for vinegar fermentation at a high temperature such 38-40 degrees C, where mesophilic strains showed no growth. They oxidized higher concentrations of ethanol up to 9% without any appreciable lag time, while alcohol oxidation with mesophilic strains was delayed or became almost impossible under such conditions. Several useful Gluconobacter species of thermotolerant acetic acid bacteria are also found, especially L-erythrulose-producing strains and cyclic alcohol-oxidizing strains. Gluconobacter frateurii CHM 43 is able to rapidly oxidize meso-erythritol at 37 degrees C leading to the accumulation of L-erythrulose, which may replace dihydroxyacetone in cosmetics. G. frateuriiCHM 9 is able to oxidize cyclic alcohols to their corresponding cyclic ketones or aliphatic ketones, which are known to be useful for preparing many different physiologically active compounds such as oxidized steroids or oxidized bicyclic ketones. The enzymes involved in these meso-erythritol and cyclic alcohol oxidations have been purified and shown to be a similar type of membrane-bound quinoproteins, consisting of a high molecular weight single peptide. This is completely different from another quinoprotein, alcohol dehydrogenase of acetic acid bacteria, which consists of three subunits including hemoproteins.

citations.title: Vinegar-processed Schisandra Chinensis enhanced therapeutic effects on colitis-induced depression through tryptophan metabolism.
citations.abstract: Background: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is an inflammatory bowel disease characterized by its incurable nature and undefined etiology, which is often accompanied by a high prevalence of comorbid depression. The gut-brain axis has emerged as a promising treatment target in recent years. Purpose: This study aimed to investigate how vinegar-processed Schisandra Chinensis (VSC) enhances therapeutic effects on depressive behavior in chronic UC mice. Methods: A chronic UC model was induced in mice using dextran sulfate sodium. The therapeutic effects of both raw and vinegar-processed Schisandra Chinensis on UC and associated depressive symptoms were assessed. Colonic mucosal damage was evaluated using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and Alcian blue staining. The integrity of the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and synaptic structures was visualized via transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) was employed to quantify inflammatory cytokine levels in the colon, serum, and brain, while western blotting was performed for protein expression analysis. Additionally, metagenomic analysis was conducted to investigate gut microbiota composition. Nissl staining and immunofluorescence were used to assess hippocampal neuronal damage, and behavioral assessments including the morris water maze, open field test, forced swimming test and tail suspension test, were implemented to evaluate depressive states. Serum metabolites were analyzed using UPLC-MS/MS. Results: Both raw and vinegar-processed Schisandra Chinensis significantly upregulated aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR), inhibited NF-κB p-p65 activation, and reduced levels of pro-inflammatory cytokine. These treatments also enhanced the expression of tight junction proteins, restored colonic mucosal and BBB integrity, alleviated damage to hippocampal neurons, and improved synaptic structure. Behavioral assessments indicated that VSC was particularly effective in ameliorating depressive-like behaviors in chronic UC mice. In the gut, both treatments reshaped the gut microbial composition, restoring the relative abundance of Duncaniella, Candidatus_Amulumruptor, Alistipes, Parabacteroides, Lachnospiraceae_bacterium, uncultured_Bacteroides_sp., Candidatus_Amulumruptor_caecigallinarius, with VSC showing more pronounced effects. Serum metabolomics revealed an increase in tryptophan levels and a decrease in kynurenine and xanthurenic acid levels with VSC, indicating that tryptophan metabolism shifted from the kynurenine pathway to the 5-HT or indole pathway. However, this phenomenon did not occur with Schisandra Chinensis (SC). Conclusion: This study demonstrated that the disruption of tryptophan metabolic balance served as a biological mechanism underlying the occurrence of depressive behaviors induced by UC. The application of SC following vinegar processing enhanced its regulatory effects on gut microbiota and tryptophan metabolism. This findings provided a new insight for the clinical management of gut-brain comorbidities.

citations.title: Gustatory Processing in Drosophila melanogaster.
citations.abstract: The ability to identify nutrient-rich food and avoid toxic substances is essential for an animal's survival. Although olfaction and vision contribute to food detection, the gustatory system acts as a final checkpoint control for food acceptance or rejection. The vinegar fly Drosophila melanogaster tastes many of the same stimuli as mammals and provides an excellent model system for comparative studies of taste detection. The relative simplicity of the fly brain and behaviors, along with the molecular genetic and functional approaches available in this system, allow the examination of gustatory neural circuits from sensory input to motor output. This review discusses the molecules and cells that detect taste compounds in the periphery and the circuits that process taste information in the brain. These studies are providing insight into how the detection of taste compounds regulates feeding decisions.

citations.title: Safety and side effects of apple vinegar intake and its effect on metabolic parameters and body weight: a systematic review.
citations.abstract: Introduction: Apple vinegar (AV) has been proclaimed to have different health benefits, such as a weight loss, the ability to lower blood glucose levels, and reducing the risk of heart diseases. Studies on animals have demonstrated effects of AV consumption, deepening our knowledge of the beneficial effects and side effects. Aim: The aims of this study were to evaluate the evidence of the effect of AV on metabolic parameters and body weight in humans, furthermore, to evaluate the safety and side effects of ingesting AV, and additionally to evaluate the evidence of the effect of AV on metabolic parameters, safety, and side effects of AV from studies performed on animals (mammals). Methods: A systematic literature search was performed. The databases PubMed (MEDLINE), PsycInfo (Ebsco), CINAHL (Ebsco), and Embase (Ovid) were searched for relevant articles. Primary outcomes were glycated hemoglobin, postprandial glucose, and synonyms for blood glucose. Secondary outcomes were waist circumference, visceral fat, high-density lipoprotein, low-density lipoprotein, triglycerides, and total cholesterol. Studies performed on humans and animals were included. The included studies performed on humans were quality assessed for risk of bias using a version of the Cochrane Collaboration's tool. Results: A total of 487 papers were identified in the literature search. Of these, 13 studies performed on humans and 12 studies performed on animals were included. There may be beneficial health effects from the consumption of AV. The risk of side effects when ingested in recommended quantities and in recommended ways seems inconsiderable. Conclusion: Due to inadequate research of high quality, the evidence for the health effects of AV is insufficient. Therefore, more large-scale, long-term clinical studies with a low risk of bias are needed before definitive conclusions can be made.

citations.title: The therapeutic importance of acid-base balance.
citations.abstract: Baking soda and vinegar have been used as home remedies for generations and today we are only a mouse-click away from claims that baking soda, lemon juice, and apple cider vinegar are miracles cures for everything from cancer to COVID-19. Despite these specious claims, the therapeutic value of controlling acid-base balance is indisputable and is the basis of Food and Drug Administration-approved treatments for constipation, epilepsy, metabolic acidosis, and peptic ulcers. In this narrative review, we present evidence in support of the current and potential therapeutic value of countering local and systemic acid-base imbalances, several of which do in fact involve the administration of baking soda (sodium bicarbonate). Furthermore, we discuss the side effects of pharmaceuticals on acid-base balance as well as the influence of acid-base status on the pharmacokinetic properties of drugs. Our review considers all major organ systems as well as information relevant to several clinical specialties such as anesthesiology, infectious disease, oncology, dentistry, and surgery.

name: Sodium Percarbonate
scoreRationale: A chlorine-free bleach that breaks down to soda, water and oxygen; the powder can damage eyes and is harmful if swallowed.
summary: Sodium percarbonate is "oxygen bleach": it releases hydrogen peroxide in water to lift stains, then breaks down harmlessly.

physical.solubility: Soluble in water, releasing hydrogen peroxide

overview: Sodium percarbonate is a crystal that holds hydrogen peroxide inside a sodium carbonate lattice, in a ratio of two Na₂CO₃ to three H₂O₂. It's essentially solid hydrogen peroxide: stable as a dry powder, but it separates into its two components as soon as it dissolves.
That gives two cleaning agents in one scoop: hydrogen peroxide to oxidize stains and sodium carbonate to raise the pH and soften the water. It's the active ingredient in “oxygen bleach” boosters.
profile.function: Removes stains, whitens laundry and deodorizes without chlorine.

mechanisms.title: Oxidizing stains
mechanisms.chemical: Released hydrogen peroxide oxidizes the conjugated chromophores in colored stains, breaking their double-bond systems.
mechanisms.biological: Coffee, wine and grass stains lose their color without the harshness of chlorine bleach.

mechanisms.title: Cold-water bleaching with an activator
mechanisms.chemical: Detergents add TAED, which reacts with peroxide (perhydrolysis) to form peracetic acid, a stronger oxidizer at low temperature.
mechanisms.biological: Clothes can be bleached at 30–40 °C instead of 60 °C or more, saving energy.

reactions.title: Dissolving
reactions.summary: The crystal comes apart in water.

steps.name: Water
steps.text: Water molecules break up the crystal lattice.

steps.name: Release
steps.text: Hydrogen peroxide and sodium carbonate dissolve separately.

steps.name: Activation
steps.text: The carbonate raises the pH, which helps the peroxide react with stains.

reactions.result: Oxygen bleach works best in warm water, or with an activator in cool water.

reactions.title: Perhydrolysis with TAED
reactions.summary: Making a stronger bleach on the spot.

steps.name: Attack
steps.text: Perhydroxyl ions (HOO⁻) from peroxide attack TAED's acetyl groups.

steps.name: Transfer
steps.text: Acetyl groups transfer to the peroxide.

steps.name: Product
steps.text: Peracetic acid forms, which bleaches effectively at low temperatures.

reactions.result: This is why many European detergents clean well at low wash temperatures.

regulatory.status: Danger: may intensify fire (H272), harmful if swallowed (H302), causes serious eye damage (H318).
Accepted as a bleaching agent in eco-labeled detergents.

hazards.title: Serious eye damage
hazards.summary: The dry powder is the main hazard.
hazards.chemical: Peroxide plus high pH damages the surface of the eye.
hazards.biological: Keep powder away from eyes and children; rinse immediately if exposed.

hazards.title: Oxidizer
hazards.summary: Store away from heat and flammable materials.
hazards.chemical: It releases oxygen as it decomposes.
hazards.biological: Oxygen can intensify a fire, so the powder shouldn't be stored near fuels.

profile.dosage: Laundry boosters are often 50–90%.

myths.claim: Oxygen bleach is just as harsh as chlorine bleach.
myths.consensus: It works more gently and breaks down to harmless products, though it's slower as a disinfectant.

environment.biodegradability: Breaks down to carbonate, water and oxygen.

synthesis.title: Crystallization
synthesis.summary: Made by combining two common chemicals.
synthesis.mechanism: Sodium carbonate solution is crystallized with hydrogen peroxide, then the crystals are coated (for example with sodium sulfate) to improve storage stability.

citations.title: Study on the catalytic degradation of Acid Orange 7 and the potential mechanism by ferrous-percarbonate.
citations.abstract: Factors affecting the degradation of Acid Orange 7 (AO7) were evaluated and optimized when ferrous was used to catalyze percarbonate in the present study. The optimized conditions included the initial pH values ranging from 3 to 11 for AO7 solution, the initial level of AO7, sodium percarbonate (SPC), and Fe2+ . Some ions and natural organic materials, which commonly exist in natural water, were also tested to evaluate their potential impacts on the degradation of AO7. The degradation efficiency of AO7 was up to 95% under the optimized test conditions, where the ferrous/percarbonate/AO7 molar ratio was 15/10/1 in the 0.285 mmol/l AO7 aqueous solution. The presence of Cl- , SO4 2- , NO3 - , Na+ , and Mg2+ did not affect the removal of AO7. The addition of HCO3 - significantly inhibited its removal, even when the concentration of HCO3 - was low to 0.6 mmol/l. A slight inhibition effect was observed when the added concentration of humic acid ranged from 0.5 to 5 mg/l, whereas the residue of AO7 was significantly enhanced when the level of humic acid was continually increased from 50 to 100 mg/l. Hydroxyl radicals (•OH) were the main reactive intermediates controlling the oxidation of AO7 in the present Fe2+ /SPC system. The produced intermediates through the degradation of AO7 were identified to include 2-coumaranone, 2-naphthol, phthalic acid, phthalimide, N-methylnaphthylamine, and 2-methylphenol. The proposed degradation pathways are consistent with the radical formation and the identified intermediates. PRACTITIONER POINTS: The ferrous/percarbonate system can remove 95% of AO7 under the optimized conditions. AO7 removal was inhibited by adding HCO3 - and humic acid, but not affected by Cl- , SO4 2- , NO3 - , Na+ , and Mg2+ . Hydroxylation, ring opening, and mineralization driven by the generated hydroxyl radicals were derived as the major processes for degrading AO7.

citations.title: Enhanced degradation of benzene by percarbonate activated with Fe(II)-glutamate complex.
citations.abstract: Effective degradation of benzene was achieved in sodium percarbonate (SPC)/Fe(II)-Glu system. The presence of glutamate (Glu) could enhance the regeneration of Fe(III) to Fe(II), which ensures the benzene degradation efficiency at wider pH range and eliminate the influence of HCO3 (-) in low concentration. Meanwhile, the significant scavenging effects of high HCO3 (-) concentration could also be overcome by increasing the Glu/SPC/Fe(II)/benzene molar ratio. Free radical probe compound tests, free radical scavenger tests, and electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) analysis were conducted to explore the reaction mechanism for benzene degradation, in which hydroxyl radical (HO•) and superoxide anion radical (O2 (•-)) were confirmed as the predominant species responsible for benzene degradation. In addition, the results obtained in actual groundwater test strongly indicated that SPC/Fe(II)-Glu system is applicable for the remediation of benzene-contaminated groundwater in practice.

citations.title: A review on percarbonate-based advanced oxidation processes for remediation of organic compounds in water.
citations.abstract: Sodium percarbonate (SPC) is considered a potential alternative to liquid hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) in organic compounds contaminated water/soil remediation due to its regularly, transportable, economical, and eco-friendly features. The solid state of SPC makes it more suitable to remediate actual soil and water with a milder H2O2 release rate. Apart from its good oxidative capacity, alkaline SPC can simultaneously remediate acidized solution and soil to the neutral condition. Conventionally, percarbonate-based advanced oxidation process (P-AOPs) system proceed through the catalysis under ultraviolet ray, transition metal ions (i.e., Fe2+, Fe3+, and V4+), and nanoscale zero-valent metals (iron, zinc, copper, and nickel). The hydroxyl radical (•OH), superoxide radical (•O2-), and carbonate radical anion (•CO3-) generated from sodium percarbonate could attack the organic pollutant structure. In this review, we present the advances of P-AOPs in heterogeneous and homogeneous catalytic processes through a wide range of activation methods. This review aims to give an overview of the catalysis and application of P-AOPs for emerging contaminants degradation and act as a guideline of the field advances. Various activation methods of percarbonate are summarized, and the influence factors in the solution matrix such as pH, anions, and cations are thoroughly discussed. Moreover, this review helps to clarify the advantages and shortcomings of P-AOPs in current scientific progress and guide the future practical direction of P-AOPs in sustainable carbon catalysis and green chemistry.

citations.title: Bleaching of nonvital teeth. A clinically relevant literature review.
citations.abstract: Today, the bleaching of nonvital, discolored teeth is a low-risk routine treatment for improving esthetics. This review article focuses on the etiology of tooth discolorations, different treatment techniques, and risks of bleaching procedures. Some tooth discolorations in endodontically treated teeth are caused by dental treatments. The three most popular techniques for nonvital tooth bleaching are the walking bleach technique, inside/outside bleaching, and in-office bleaching. The walking bleach technique is a relatively reliable, fairly simple technique for dentists and patients. Inside/outside bleaching can be used additionally when internal and external bleaching must be combined. In-office bleaching seems to be a short-term solution, the effects of which can largely be attributed to dehydration of the teeth. There are still some open questions concerning the bleaching agents. Improved safety seems desirable with regard to adding thiourea as a scavenger of radicals or newer materials such as sodium percarbonate. The thermocatalytic technique, insufficient cervical sealing, and high concentrations of bleaching agents should be avoided, as this can increase the risk of cervical root resorptions. Patients should be informed about the low predictability of bleaching success and the risk of recurrent discoloration. The risk of cervical root resorption should be discussed with the patient. There is a strong correlation between root resorption and dental trauma.

citations.title: Advances in Controlled Oxygen Generating Biomaterials for Tissue Engineering and Regenerative Therapy.
citations.abstract: Oxygen (O2) generating biomaterials are emerging as important compositions to improve our capabilities in supporting tissue engineering and regenerative therapeutics. Several in vitro studies demonstrated the usefulness of O2 releasing biomaterials in enhancing cell survival and differentiation. However, more efforts are needed to develop materials that can provide sustained O2 release for the long-term. In this paper, we present different O2 generating sources, including hydrogen peroxide, sodium percarbonate, calcium peroxide and magnesium peroxide, and also cover types of carriers and relevant methods of fabricating O2 generating systems. Then, the applications of O2 generating materials in supporting engineered constructs, supplying high O2 demanding cell transplants, and supporting ischemic tissues are discussed. Moreover, the challenges and future perspectives are highlighted.

name: Sodium Dodecylbenzenesulfonate
scoreRationale: The world's most-used detergent surfactant: readily biodegradable, but a skin and eye irritant and harmful to aquatic life before treatment.
summary: LAS is the main cleaning agent in most laundry detergents. It biodegrades well but irritates skin and eyes.

physical.state: White to yellow powder or paste
physical.phStability: Stable across pH; tolerant of hard water with builders

overview: Sodium dodecylbenzenesulfonate is the most-used member of the linear alkylbenzene sulfonates (LAS), the world's workhorse detergent surfactants. It has a straight 12-carbon chain attached to a benzene ring that carries a negatively charged sulfonate group (–SO₃⁻).

The straight chain matters. Early detergents used branched chains that bacteria couldn't break down, causing mountains of foam on rivers in the 1950s and 60s. Switching to linear chains, which microbes digest from the end, made LAS readily biodegradable.
profile.function: Lifts and suspends oily soils in laundry and dish detergents.

mechanisms.title: Detergency
mechanisms.chemical: LAS adsorbs onto fabric and oily soil, lowering interfacial tension so oil rolls up into droplets and lifts off into micelles.
mechanisms.biological: Greasy stains wash out of clothes, and the negative charges keep removed soil from settling back on fabric.

mechanisms.title: Biodegradation
mechanisms.chemical: Bacteria oxidize the end of the straight chain, then shorten it two carbons at a time by beta-oxidation, the same pathway that breaks down fats, before opening the ring.
mechanisms.biological: Most LAS is removed in wastewater treatment within days, protecting rivers.

mechanisms.title: Skin and eye irritation
mechanisms.chemical: Like other anionic surfactants, LAS extracts lipids and binds proteins at the skin surface.
mechanisms.biological: Undiluted detergent can redden skin and seriously irritate eyes.

reactions.title: Sulfonation
reactions.summary: Attaching a charged head to an oily tail.

steps.name: Electrophile
steps.text: Sulfur trioxide is a powerful electrophile.

steps.name: Substitution
steps.text: It attacks the benzene ring of linear alkylbenzene, swapping a hydrogen for a –SO₃H group (electrophilic aromatic substitution).

steps.name: Neutralization
steps.text: Sodium hydroxide converts the sulfonic acid into its sodium salt.

reactions.result: Electrophilic aromatic substitution is one of the main reactions of benzene rings.

regulatory.status: Surfactants must meet ready-biodegradability criteria, which LAS does.
Warning: harmful if swallowed, causes skin irritation and serious eye damage; harmful to aquatic life.

hazards.title: Eye damage from concentrated detergent
hazards.summary: Especially a risk with liquid detergent pods.
hazards.chemical: Concentrated surfactant disrupts corneal cells.
hazards.biological: Eye exposure needs prolonged rinsing; detergent pods should be kept away from young children.

hazards.title: Harm to aquatic life before treatment
hazards.summary: Wastewater treatment removes most of it.
hazards.chemical: Surfactants disrupt the gill membranes of fish and invertebrates.
hazards.biological: Untreated discharges can harm aquatic life, which is why biodegradability is legally required for detergents in the EU.

profile.dosage: Laundry detergents contain about 5–25%.

myths.claim: Detergent foam in rivers means detergents don't biodegrade.
myths.consensus: That was true of branched ABS in the 1950s; linear LAS replaced it and degrades within days.

environment.biodegradability: Readily biodegradable (aerobic); persists longer in anaerobic sediments.
environment.aquaticToxicity: Harmful to aquatic life before wastewater treatment.

synthesis.title: From petroleum
synthesis.summary: Built in two main steps.
synthesis.mechanism: Benzene is alkylated with linear C10–C14 olefins to make linear alkylbenzene, which is sulfonated with sulfur trioxide and neutralized with sodium hydroxide.
synthesis.significance: In 1965 the U.S. detergent industry switched from branched to linear surfactants to end the foam problem on rivers.

citations.title: Characteristics and pH-Responsiveness of SDBS-Stabilized Crude Oil/Water Nanoemulsions.
citations.abstract: Nanoemulsions are colloidal systems with a wide spectrum of applications in several industrial fields. In this study, crude oil-in-water (O/W) nanoemulsions were formulated using different dosages of the anionic sodium dodecylbenzenesulfonate (SDBS) surfactant. The formulated nanoemulsions were characterized in terms of emulsion droplet size, zeta potential, and interfacial tension (IFT). Additionally, the rheological behavior, long-term stability, and on-demand breakdown of the nanoemulsions via a pH-responsive mechanism were evaluated. The obtained results revealed the formation of as low as 63.5 nm average droplet size with a narrow distribution (33-142 nm). Additionally, highly negative zeta potential (i.e., -62.2 mV) and reasonably low IFT (0.45 mN/m) were obtained at 4% SDBS. The flow-ability of the nanoemulsions was also investigated and the obtained results revealed an increase in the nanoemulsion viscosity with increasing the emulsifier content. Nonetheless, even at the highest SDBS dosage of 4%, the nanoemulsion viscosity at ambient conditions never exceeded 2.5 mPa·s. A significant reduction in viscosity was obtained with increasing the nanoemulsion temperature. The formulated nanoemulsions displayed extreme stability with no demulsification signs irrespective of the emulsifier dosage even after one-month shelf-life. Another interesting and, yet, surprising observation reported herein is the pH-induced demulsification despite SDBS not possessing a pH-responsive character. This behavior enabled the on-demand breakdown of the nanoemulsions by simply altering their pH via the addition of HCl or NaOH; a complete and quick oil separation can be achieved using this simple and cheap demulsification method. The obtained results reveal the potential utilization of the formulated nanoemulsions in oilfield-related applications such as enhanced oil recovery (EOR), well stimulation and remediation, well-bore cleaning, and formation fracturing.

citations.title: Ultrahigh-throughput screening system for directed polymer binding peptide evolution.
citations.abstract: Accumulation of plastics in the environment became a geological indicator of the Anthropocene era. An effective reduction of long-lasting plastics requires a treatment with micro-organisms that release polymer-degrading enzymes. Polymer binding peptides function as adhesion promoters and enable a targeted binding of whole cells to polymer surfaces. An esterase A-based Escherichia coli cell surface display screening system was developed, that enabled directed evolution of polymer binding peptides for improved binding strength to polymers. The E. coli cell surface screening system facilitates an enrichment of improved binding peptides from a culture broth through immobilization of whole cells on polymer beads. The polypropylene (PP)-binding peptide liquid chromatography peak I (LCI) was simultaneously saturated at five positions (Y29, D31, G35, E42, and D45; 3.2 million variants) and screened for improved PP-binding in the presence of the anionic surfactant sodium dodecylbenzenesulfonate (LAS; 0.25 mM). The cell surface system enabled efficient screening of the generated LCI diversity (in total ~10 million clones were screened). Characterization of identified LCI binders revealed an up to 12-fold improvement (eGFP-LCI-CSD-3: E42V/D45H) in PP-binding strength in the presence of the surfactant LAS (0.125 mM). The latter represents a first whole cell display screening system to improve adhesion peptides which can be used to direct and to immobilize organisms specifically to polymer surfaces (e.g., PP) and novel applications (e.g., in targeted plastic degradation).

citations.title: Amended safety assessment of dodecylbenzenesulfonate, decylbenzenesulfonate, and tridecylbenzenesulfonate salts as used in cosmetics.
citations.abstract: Sodium dodecylbenzenesulfonate is one of a group of salts of alkylbenzene sulfonates used in cosmetics as surfactant-cleansing agents. Sodium dodecylbenzenesulfonate is soluble in water and partially soluble in alcohol, with dermal absorption dependent on pH. Dodecylbenzenesulfonate salts are not toxic in single-dose oral and dermal animal tests, and no systemic toxicities were observed in repeat-dose dermal animal studies. In dermal animal studies, no evidence of reproductive or developmental toxicity was reported. At 15% concentrations, sodium dodecylbenzenesulfonate was severely irritating to rabbit skin. The Cosmetic Ingredient Review Expert Panel concluded that the irritant properties of these ingredients are similar to those of other detergents, with severity dependent on concentration and pH. Products containing these ingredients should be formulated to ensure that the irritancy potential is minimized.

citations.title: Organic Acid Sanitizers for Natamycin and Other Fungicides in Recirculating Application Systems for Citrus Postharvest Decay Management.
citations.abstract: Natamycin is a new postharvest biofungicide for citrus and some other fruit crops in the United States that can be effectively used in recycling drench or flooder treatments. These applications necessitate sanitation of the fungicide solution to ensure that it remains free from contamination by bacteria that are potentially human pathogens. During in vitro experiments, heated (48°C) citric acid (1,100 or 2,200 μg/ml) amended with sodium dodecylbenzenesulfonate (SDBS) (60 or 120 μg/ml, respectively) significantly reduced the viability of a nonpathogenic strain of Escherichia coli in natamycin solutions by >5 log10 compared with the control. During laboratory studies with Penicillium digitatum-inoculated lemon fruit, 1,000 μg/ml of natamycin mixed with 1,000 μg/ml of lactic acid or citric acid and with or without SDBS (55 μg/ml) effectively and significantly reduced green mold. Natamycin mixed with lactic acid at ≥2,000 μg/ml, however, caused fruit injury, resulting in browning and rind pitting. Natamycin was incompatible with peroxyacetic acid, resulting in reduced efficacy against green mold. Sodium hypochlorite mixed with natamycin lost its toxicity to E. coli; however, the performance of natamycin was not affected. With heated (average 49°C) drench treatments on an experimental packing line, natamycin (1,000 μg/ml), fludioxonil (300 μg/ml), or azoxystrobin (300 μg/ml) mixed with citric acid (1,000 μg/ml) and SDBS (55 μg/ml) were effective against green mold without fruit injury. At a pH between 3.6 and 3.8, citric acid-SDBS significantly reduced the viability of E. coli by approximately 4 log10 in mixtures with fludioxonil or azoxystrobin, but not with natamycin. However, natamycin at 1,000 μg/ml mixed with 2,000 μg/ml of citric acid and SDBS (55 μg/ml) significantly reduced E. coli counts by >4 log10 within 4 min when the pH was maintained between 3.0 and 3.3, and the efficacy of the fungicide was retained. The use of citric acid with a surfactant can be a viable alternative sanitation method for natamycin in citrus packinghouses utilizing heated recirculating fungicide systems.

citations.title: In Situ Assay of Interfacial Interaction between ZnO Nanoparticles and Live Cell Disturbed by Surfactants.
citations.abstract: The interfacial interaction between pollutants and organisms is a critical process in controlling the environmental fates of pollutants; however, in situ assay of the interaction is still a great challenge. Here, in situ determination of dissociation constants (Kd) for ZnO nanoparticles (ZnO NPs) from live algal cells disturbed by different-charged surfactants was established using microscale thermophoresis (MST). Moreover, in situ measurement of the adhesion force between the ZnO NPs probe and live single cell was performed using an atomic force microscope (AFM). Results showed that the cationic cetyltrimethylammonium chloride (CTAC) and anionic sodium dodecylbenzenesulfonate (SDBS) increased but nonionic Triton X-100 (TX-100) decreased the adhesion of ZnO NPs on cells. However, the force signature exhibited a smooth single retracted peak at short distances in the SDBS- and TX-100-treated groups, distinguished from the "see-saw" pattern peak in the CTAC-treated groups. The extended Derjaguin-Landau-Verway-Overbeek (XDLVO) calculation further confirmed that SDBS and TX-100 mainly disturbed the short-range hydration on the NP-cell interface, while CTAC reduced the long-range electrostatic repulsion. Furthermore, an excellent linear correlation between Zn bioaccumulation and two parameters (Kd and adhesion force) indicated that NP-cell interfacial interactions affected Zn bioaccumulation. Thus, in situ assay provides a quantitative basis for the pollutant-organism interfacial interaction to evaluate the environmental fate and ecological risk of pollutants.

name: Limonene
scoreRationale: A natural citrus solvent, but it oxidizes into skin sensitizers and reacts with indoor ozone to form formaldehyde and fine particles.
summary: Limonene gives cleaners and cosmetics a citrus scent and dissolves grease. Natural, but aged limonene is a common skin allergen.

physical.state: Colorless oily liquid with orange scent
physical.solubility: Insoluble in water; miscible with oils and alcohol

overview: Limonene is a naturally occurring monoterpene (C₁₀H₁₆) and the primary component of essential oils extracted from citrus rinds. As a highly volatile compound, it vaporizes easily at room temperature, which is why peeling an orange instantly releases a strong, distinct scent.

Limonene exists as two mirror-image isomers (enantiomers) that trigger different olfactory receptors in the human nose. (R)-limonene (D-limonene) smells like sweet oranges and is the most abundant form in nature. (S)-limonene (L-limonene) has a harsher, pine-like, or turpentinic odor often associated with lemons, caraway, and pine needles.
profile.function: Dissolves grease, adhesives and tar, and adds a fresh citrus scent.

mechanisms.title: Anti-inflammatory action
mechanisms.chemical: Inside a cell's cytoplasm, a protein complex called NF-κB is normally kept inactive by being bound to an inhibitor protein called IκB. When a cell is stressed, enzymes try to break down IκB to free NF-κB. Limonene molecules diffuse across the cell membrane and chemically interfere with this breakdown, preventing IκB from being degraded.
mechanisms.biological: Because IκB isn't broken down, NF-κB remains locked in the cytoplasm and cannot enter the cell's nucleus. Since it can't reach the DNA, it cannot trigger the genes responsible for creating pro-inflammatory cytokines (like TNF-α and IL-6). The result is a systemic reduction in swelling, redness, and immune cell overreaction at the tissue level.

mechanisms.title: Antioxidant properties
mechanisms.chemical: The limonene molecule (C₁₀H₁₆) contains two carbon-carbon double bonds (alkenes). These double bonds are rich in electrons. When a highly reactive free radical (an unstable molecule missing an electron, such as a hydroxyl radical) enters the environment, limonene easily donates an electron or undergoes an addition reaction. This neutralizes the radical without turning limonene into a dangerous radical itself.
mechanisms.biological: By intercepting these free radicals, limonene acts as a cellular shield. It prevents “lipid peroxidation”, a process where free radicals steal electrons from the lipids in cell membranes, causing the membrane to collapse. This protects tissues from oxidative stress, cellular aging, and DNA damage.

mechanisms.title: Gastrointestinal and reflux relief
mechanisms.chemical: D-limonene is highly lipophilic (fat-loving) and hydrophobic (water-repelling). It also has a specific gravity of around 0.84, making it significantly lighter than water. In the highly acidic, watery environment of the stomach, limonene does not dissolve.
mechanisms.biological: Because it cannot mix with stomach acid and is lighter than water, limonene floats to the top of the gastric juices. It forms a buoyant, protective lipid layer. If the stomach contents splash upward, this lipid raft coats the lower esophageal sphincter, creating a physical barrier that protects the sensitive esophagus tissue from acid burns (reflux). It also acts as a mild localized solvent to break down stagnant mucus and promotes normal stomach muscle contractions (peristalsis).

mechanisms.title: Hepatic (liver) enzyme induction
mechanisms.chemical: Once in the bloodstream, limonene reaches the liver and enters hepatocytes (liver cells). There, it acts as a ligand (a binding molecule), attaching to specific intracellular receptors like the Constitutive Androstane Receptor (CAR). This binding triggers the cell's machinery to transcribe mRNA for specific detoxification enzymes.
mechanisms.biological: The liver ramps up its production of Phase I (cytochrome P450) and Phase II (like glutathione S-transferase) enzymes. When fat-soluble toxins enter the liver, Phase I enzymes slightly modify them, and Phase II enzymes attach a large, water-soluble molecule to them. Thanks to limonene jump-starting this system, dangerous toxins are rapidly converted into safe, water-soluble waste that the kidneys can easily filter out into urine.

reactions.title: Autooxidation (reaction with oxygen over time)
reactions.summary: Autooxidation is a spontaneous, radical-chain reaction that happens when limonene is exposed to oxygen in the air, especially in the presence of light or heat (which act as initiators). Pure limonene itself rarely causes skin allergies, but its autooxidation products are well-known contact allergens.

steps.name: Initiation
steps.text: A trace free radical (often generated by UV light) abstracts a hydrogen atom from an allylic carbon on the limonene ring (a carbon right next to a double bond). This leaves behind a limonene radical.

steps.name: Propagation
steps.text: This highly reactive limonene radical instantly reacts with molecular oxygen (O₂) from the air, forming a peroxy radical (–OO•).

steps.name: Hydroperoxide formation
steps.text: The peroxy radical steals a hydrogen atom from another intact limonene molecule, creating limonene hydroperoxide (R–OOH) and a new limonene radical to keep the chain reaction going.

steps.name: Decomposition
steps.text: The hydroperoxides are relatively unstable. Over time, they break down into secondary oxidation products, most notably carvone (a ketone), carveol (an alcohol), and limonene oxide (an epoxide).

reactions.result: When an old bottle of citrus essential oil sits on a sunny shelf, the limonene inside is slowly converting into hydroperoxides and carvone, which is why older oils can cause skin rashes (contact dermatitis).

reactions.title: Indoor ozone chemistry (ozonolysis)
reactions.summary: When you use citrus-scented cleaning sprays indoors, the limonene in the air reacts quickly with indoor ozone (O₃). Ozone is a highly reactive gas that often seeps in from outdoor smog or is generated by certain air purifiers and laser printers. The reaction follows the Criegee pathway.

steps.name: Cycloaddition
steps.text: The ozone molecule (O₃) attacks one of limonene's double bonds (usually the endocyclic one, the bond inside the main ring) in a concerted reaction. It forms a highly unstable, five-membered ring structure called a primary ozonide.

steps.name: Cleavage
steps.text: The primary ozonide instantly collapses, breaking the original carbon-carbon double bond completely. This creates two fragments: a carbonyl compound and a highly energetic molecule called a Criegee intermediate (a carbonyl oxide).

steps.name: Secondary reactions
steps.text: The Criegee intermediate is extremely unstable. It quickly undergoes further reactions (often reacting with water vapor in the air or rearranging itself) to form a variety of oxidized volatile organic compounds (VOCs).

steps.name: Aerosol formation
steps.text: The large, oxygenated molecules created in this process have very low vapor pressure. Instead of staying as gases, they rapidly condense onto dust particles or clump together to form microscopic liquid or solid droplets suspended in the air.

reactions.result: This reaction produces Secondary Organic Aerosols (SOAs), ultrafine particles that are easily inhaled deep into the lungs. The reaction also produces small amounts of formaldehyde and hydroxyl radicals (OH•). This is why atmospheric chemists often warn that aggressively scrubbing a poorly ventilated room with pine or citrus cleaners on a high-ozone (smoggy) day actually creates a burst of indoor air pollution.

regulatory.status: Must be named on labels above 0.001% (leave-on) or 0.01% (rinse-off) as a fragrance allergen.
Generally Recognized as Safe as a flavoring.
Warning: flammable, skin irritant and sensitizer, very toxic to aquatic life.

hazards.title: Skin sensitization (contact dermatitis)
hazards.summary: Fresh, pure limonene is rarely a skin irritant. The danger arises when the chemical ages.
hazards.chemical: Autooxidation: when a bottle of citrus essential oil or cleaner is opened and exposed to ambient air, light and room temperatures, limonene undergoes spontaneous autooxidation. Oxygen from the air attacks the molecule's double bonds, converting the benign limonene into limonene hydroperoxides (along with carvone and limonene oxide).
hazards.biological: Haptenation: these hydroperoxides are highly reactive sensitizers. Being small and fat-soluble, they easily cross the skin's outer barrier (the stratum corneum). Once inside, they act as “haptens”, molecules that covalently bind to the skin's natural proteins. The immune system's Langerhans cells detect these altered proteins as foreign invaders and mount a Type IV delayed immune response, resulting in the red, blistering rash known as allergic contact dermatitis.

hazards.title: Respiratory irritation
hazards.summary: Limonene itself is a pleasant scent, but it acts as a precursor to indoor air pollution.
hazards.chemical: Ozonolysis: when limonene vapor from cleaning sprays mixes with indoor ozone (often generated by smog, laser printers or air purifiers), it undergoes rapid ozonolysis. The ozone breaks the limonene ring apart, creating formaldehyde, highly reactive radicals, and large, oxidized volatile organic compounds.
hazards.biological: Oxidative stress: because the newly formed oxidized compounds are heavy, they condense out of the gas phase into microscopic droplets called Secondary Organic Aerosols (SOAs). When a person breathes this air, the ultrafine aerosols and formaldehyde penetrate deep into the lungs. They induce localized oxidative stress, irritating the mucous membranes and potentially triggering coughing, dyspnea and asthma flare-ups.

hazards.title: Aspiration hazard
hazards.summary: Though its oral toxicity is very low, swallowing concentrated limonene (like a pure essential oil or degreaser) poses a mechanical and biological threat to the lungs.
hazards.chemical: Physical properties: limonene is a non-polar hydrocarbon with very low viscosity (it is very thin) and low surface tension.
hazards.biological: Surfactant destruction: if a person swallows concentrated limonene and then accidentally chokes or vomits, the chemical's low surface tension allows it to easily slip past the vocal cords and slide deep into the lungs (aspiration). Once inside the alveoli, the solvent rapidly dissolves the lipid-based pulmonary surfactant, the critical fluid that keeps air sacs open. This leads to massive inflammation, fluid pooling in the lungs (pulmonary edema), and a life-threatening condition called chemical pneumonitis.

hazards.title: Aquatic toxicity
hazards.summary: Limonene is heavily regulated regarding disposal because it is devastating to marine ecosystems.
hazards.chemical: Hydrophobicity: limonene has a specific gravity of roughly 0.84 and is almost entirely insoluble in water. If poured down a drain or spilled in a waterway, it does not dilute; it floats on the surface, forming a persistent, concentrated lipid film.
hazards.biological: Membrane disruption: limonene is classified as highly toxic to aquatic life (Aquatic Acute 1). Because it is highly lipophilic (fat-loving), the floating chemical rapidly partitions into the gills, fatty tissues and cell membranes of fish and invertebrates. This aggressive accumulation disrupts the structural integrity of their lipid membranes, causing cellular leakage, organ failure and death.

profile.dosage: Cleaners may contain 1–20%; cosmetics usually under 1%.

myths.claim: Natural citrus cleaners are completely non-toxic.
myths.consensus: Limonene is natural but still a sensitizer and an aquatic toxin.

environment.notes: A volatile organic compound that contributes to indoor air pollution chemistry.

synthesis.title: Biological synthesis (how plants make it)
synthesis.summary: Plants do not build limonene from scratch in one step; they use an enzyme-driven cascade. In citrus plants, this happens inside specialized secretory cavities in the fruit peel.
synthesis.mechanism: The universal building block for monoterpenes is geranyl pyrophosphate (GPP), a 10-carbon linear molecule. The plant enzyme limonene synthase grabs a GPP molecule and forces it into a specific shape (enzymatic cyclization).
steps: The enzyme strips away the pyrophosphate group, leaving a positively charged, highly reactive carbon (a carbocation).
This unstable molecule rearranges itself into a different intermediate (the linalyl cation).
The positive charge pulls the tail of the molecule around, forcing it to snap shut into a six-carbon ring (the α-terpinyl cation).
Finally, the enzyme removes a proton (H⁺), which stabilizes the ring, creates the final double bonds, and releases pure (R)-limonene.
synthesis.significance: This is a highly stereospecific reaction. Because the enzyme's “pocket” is perfectly shaped, it almost exclusively produces the (R)-enantiomer (sweet orange scent) in citrus, whereas a different enzyme in pine trees produces the (S)-enantiomer (pine scent).

synthesis.title: Chemical synthesis (the Diels–Alder reaction)
synthesis.summary: Commercially, it is much cheaper to squeeze orange peels than to synthesize limonene from scratch. However, if a chemist needs to build the molecule in a laboratory, they use a classic organic reaction called a Diels–Alder cycloaddition.
synthesis.mechanism: The starting material is isoprene, a simple 5-carbon molecule with two double bonds (a diene). Under high heat, two isoprene molecules collide. One acts as the “diene” (contributing 4 atoms) and the other acts as the “dienophile” (contributing 2 atoms to the new bond). The electrons from their double bonds shift in a synchronized, circular movement. This single concerted [4+2] cycloaddition step zips the two molecules together, forming the six-membered cyclohexene ring of limonene.
synthesis.significance: Because there is no enzyme guiding the shape, this thermal reaction produces dipentene, a 50/50 racemic mixture of both (R)-limonene and (S)-limonene. Dipentene is often used as a cheap industrial solvent or in synthetic rubber manufacturing, as separating the two enantiomers is difficult and expensive.

synthesis.title: Industrial manufacturing (physical extraction)
synthesis.summary: The vast majority of the world's commercial limonene, over 70,000 tons annually, is an upcycled byproduct of the citrus juice industry. Because limonene is already fully synthesized by the plant, the manufacturing process relies on physical separation rather than chemical reactions.
synthesis.mechanism: Centrifugation and steam distillation: when oranges are pressed for juice, the leftover peels (which contain up to 95% of the fruit's limonene) are heavily crushed. This ruptures the oil glands. The resulting slurry is washed with water and put into massive centrifuges. Because limonene is a hydrophobic hydrocarbon with a low density, the centrifuge easily spins the heavier water and plant matter outward, leaving a floating layer of cold-pressed orange oil.
synthesis.significance: If higher purity is needed (for chemical feedstocks or pharmaceuticals), this crude oil is then placed in a vacuum distillation column. Because limonene is highly volatile, it boils off at a specific temperature under a vacuum, leaving the heavier waxes and pigments behind. The vapor is then condensed back into 99% pure, industrial-grade D-limonene.

citations.title: Biotechnological production of limonene in microorganisms.
citations.abstract: This mini review describes novel, biotechnology-based, ways of producing the monoterpene limonene. Limonene is applied in relatively highly priced products, such as fragrances, and also has applications with lower value but large production volume, such as biomaterials. Limonene is currently produced as a side product from the citrus juice industry, but the availability and quality are fluctuating and may be insufficient for novel bulk applications. Therefore, complementary microbial production of limonene would be interesting. Since limonene can be derivatized to high-value compounds, microbial platforms also have a great potential beyond just producing limonene. In this review, we discuss the ins and outs of microbial limonene production in comparison with plant-based and chemical production. Achievements and specific challenges for microbial production of limonene are discussed, especially in the light of bulk applications such as biomaterials.

citations.title: The volatome of Aspergillus fumigatus.
citations.abstract: Early detection of invasive aspergillosis is absolutely required for efficient therapy of this fungal infection. The identification of fungal volatiles in patient breath can be an alternative for the detection of Aspergillus fumigatus that still remains problematic. In this work, we investigated the production of volatile organic compounds (VOCs) by A. fumigatus in vitro, and we show that volatile production depends on the nutritional environment. A. fumigatus produces a multiplicity of VOCs, predominantly terpenes and related compounds. The production of sesquiterpenoid compounds was found to be strongly induced by increased iron concentrations and certain drugs, i.e., pravastatin. Terpenes that were always detectable in large amounts were α-pinene, camphene, and limonene, as well as sesquiterpenes, identified as α-bergamotene and β-trans-bergamotene. Other substance classes that were found to be present in the volatome, such as 1-octen-3-ol, 3-octanone, and pyrazines, were found only under specific growth conditions. Drugs that interfere with the terpene biosynthesis pathway influenced the composition of the fungal volatome, and most notably, a block of sesquiterpene biosynthesis by the bisphosphonate alendronate fundamentally changed the VOC composition. Using deletion mutants, we also show that a terpene cyclase and a putative kaurene synthase are essential for the synthesis of volatile terpenes by A. fumigatus. The present analysis of in vitro volatile production by A. fumigatus suggests that VOCs may be used in the diagnosis of infections caused by this fungus.

citations.title: Botanical solvents.
citations.abstract: Botanical, or plant-derived, solvents such as turpentine, pine oils, and various essential oils are used as environmentally acceptable alternatives to traditional solvents and degreasing agents. This article focuses on three lesser-known botanical solvents: limonene, oleic acid, and linoleic acid. Although data are limited, limonene, linoleic acid, and oleic acid are likely of low toxicity. Mild skin irritation may occur from exposure to these compounds, and oxidation products of limonene may produce dermal sensitization. Limonene, and possibly linoleic and oleic acids, may have irritative and bronchoconstrictive airway effects; however, data are scant and more studies are required.

citations.title: North American Contact Dermatitis Group Patch Test Results: 2021-2022.
citations.abstract: Background: Patch testing is an important diagnostic tool for the assessment of allergic contact dermatitis (ACD). Objective: This study documents the North American Contact Dermatitis Group (NACDG) patch testing results from 2021 to 2022. Methods: At 12 centers in North America, patients were tested in a standardized manner with a screening series of 80 allergens. Results: Overall, 3056 patients were tested; 2200 (72.0%) had at least 1 positive/allergic patch test reaction and 1412 patients (46.6%) had a primary diagnosis of ACD. The most commonly positive allergens were nickel sulfate hexahydrate 5% and 2.5% petrolatum (24.9% and 22.1%, respectively), methylisothiazolinone (MI) (11.5%), hydroperoxides of linalool (10.1%), cobalt chloride hexahydrate (9.2%), and methylchloroisothiazolinone/methylisothiazolinone (9.0%). Compared with 2019-2020, prevalence of the top 20 allergens statistically increased for nickel (P < 0.001), cobalt (P < 0.01), gold (P < 0.001), hydroperoxides of limonene (P < 0.001), oleamidopropyl dimethylamine (P < 0.01), dimethylaminopropylamine (P < 0.01), and ammonium persulfate (P < 0.001). MI positivity continued to decrease from its peak in 2017-2018. More than one-fifth of patients (n = 640, 21.1%) had at least one clinically relevant reaction to an allergen/substance not present in the NACDG screening series. Conclusions: The epidemic of MI contact allergy in North America appears to continue its descent. Fragrance allergy is still very common, but the composition of fragrance allergy markers appears to be changing. Patch testing using a robust screening series, and supplemental allergens as indicated, is necessary for the comprehensive evaluation of ACD.

citations.title: Limonene Hydroperoxides.
citations.abstract: Limonene is a fragrance widely used in cosmetics and household products. Until recently, contact allergy to limonene was considered rare because positive patch tests to it were infrequently observed. In recent years, however, it has been demonstrated that exposure of limonene to oxygen (air) results in the formation of a number of oxidation products, of which the hydroperoxides have a far stronger sensitizing potency than the pure compound. By routine testing of patients suspected of contact dermatitis with hydroperoxides of limonene, high frequencies of positive reactions were found, indicating that these chemicals are important fragrance allergens. It should be realized, however, that a number of "positive" reactions may well be false-positive, irritant responses.

name: Protease
scoreRationale: Lets detergents clean at lower temperatures, but enzyme dust is a respiratory sensitizer, so products use encapsulated granules.
summary: Protease enzymes break down protein stains like blood, egg and grass. They're safe in finished detergents but can cause allergies as dust.

identity.composition: Serine protease enzymes (subtilisins) produced by Bacillus bacteria, supplied as encapsulated granules or stabilized liquids.

overview: Proteases are enzymes that cut proteins. The ones in laundry detergents are mostly subtilisins, made by Bacillus bacteria: folded protein molecules whose active site holds a precisely arranged trio of amino acids (serine, histidine and aspartate) called the catalytic triad.
Each enzyme molecule can cut thousands of peptide bonds per minute without being used up, breaking protein stains like blood, egg and grass into small fragments that wash away, even in cold water.
profile.function: Digests protein stains into small, water-soluble peptides, enabling cold-water washing.

mechanisms.title: The catalytic triad
mechanisms.chemical: Aspartate and histidine together pull a proton from serine, turning serine's oxygen into a powerful nucleophile that attacks the carbonyl carbon of a peptide bond.
mechanisms.biological: Protein stains are cut into short, water-soluble peptides at mild temperatures, so clothes come clean without hot water.

mechanisms.title: Engineered to survive bleach
mechanisms.chemical: Replacing an easily oxidized methionine near the active site with a different amino acid makes subtilisin resistant to oxidation.
mechanisms.biological: The enzyme keeps working in detergents that also contain oxygen bleach, an early success of protein engineering.

mechanisms.title: Respiratory allergy
mechanisms.chemical: Inhaled enzyme dust is recognized by the immune system as a foreign protein.
mechanisms.biological: People can develop IgE-mediated allergy and asthma, which is why enzymes are sold encapsulated or in liquids, not as loose dust.

reactions.title: Peptide-bond hydrolysis
reactions.summary: How subtilisin cuts a protein, step by step.

steps.name: Acylation
steps.text: Activated serine attacks the peptide bond's carbonyl carbon, forming a tetrahedral intermediate.

steps.name: Cleavage
steps.text: The bond breaks; one fragment leaves while the other stays attached to serine (the acyl-enzyme).

steps.name: Deacylation
steps.text: A water molecule, activated by histidine, attacks the acyl-enzyme.

steps.name: Reset
steps.text: The second fragment is released and the enzyme is ready for the next bond.

reactions.result: Enzymes are catalysts: they speed reactions enormously and come out unchanged.

regulatory.status: Danger: may cause allergy or asthma symptoms if inhaled (H334).
Manufacturers monitor workplace enzyme exposure and encapsulate enzymes to prevent dust.

hazards.title: Respiratory sensitization
hazards.summary: Mainly a workplace hazard for detergent manufacturers.
hazards.chemical: Airborne enzyme protein triggers antibody production in the lungs.
hazards.biological: Allergy and asthma symptoms in exposed workers led the industry to encapsulate enzymes and monitor air levels.

profile.dosage: Detergents contain well under 1% active enzyme protein.

myths.claim: Enzyme detergents eat your skin.
myths.consensus: They are designed for stains; consumer skin reactions are uncommon at use concentrations.

synthesis.title: Fermentation
synthesis.summary: Bacteria make detergent enzymes.
synthesis.mechanism: Engineered Bacillus strains grow in large fermenters and secrete protease into the broth. The enzyme is recovered, concentrated, and encapsulated in granules or stabilized in liquid.
synthesis.significance: Otto Röhm made the first enzyme detergent in 1913 using enzymes from animal pancreas; bacterial enzymes took over in the 1960s.
